MAGA Candidate John Sununu Wins New Hampshire GOP Primary as Epstein Email's 'Good Stories' Line Resurfaces
Sununu defeats Scott Brown but faces scrutiny over Epstein email ahead of Senate race
John Sununu is New Hampshire's Republican nominee for the US Senate, but a four-word reference in a 2010 Jeffrey Epstein email continues to shadow his campaign.
The former senator defeated rival Scott Brown in Tuesday's primary, propelled by an endorsement from President Donald Trump and a famous family name. Yet even as he claimed victory, questions kept circling back to a 2010 email from Epstein that mentioned a 'John Sununu' as having 'good stories'.
Sununu now heads into a November face-off with Democratic Representative Chris Pappas carrying both a commanding primary victory and an unresolved controversy.
Sununu Routs Brown To Claim GOP Nomination
Sununu, 62, defeated Brown on 8 September 2026, taking roughly 68 per cent of the vote to Brown's 26.9 per cent, according to results reported by NBC News and Outlook India from Associated Press tallies. The Associated Press called the race within an hour of polls closing.
Sununu, whose father and brother both served as New Hampshire governors, previously represented the state in the US House before serving in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, when he lost his re-election bid to Jeanne Shaheen. Her retirement after three terms opened the seat Sununu is now seeking to reclaim.
Trump endorsed Sununu in February 2026 despite friction dating to 2024, when Sununu backed Nikki Haley and called Trump a 'loser'. Brown, a former Massachusetts senator and Trump-appointed ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa, tried running to Sununu's right but could not close the gap, per New Hampshire Bulletin.
On the Democratic side, Pappas, 46, defeated Democratic socialist challenger Karishma Manzur with roughly 64 per cent of the vote, NBC News projected, setting up a battleground contest.
The Email That Will Not Go Away
At the centre of the campaign's most persistent storyline is a single line buried in roughly 3.5 million pages of documents released by the US Department of Justice, in an exchange between Epstein and his associate, biotech investor Boris Nikolic.
According to NH Journal, which reviewed the four-email thread, Epstein wrote to Nikolic shortly after 1:30am on 29 May 2010, suggesting they strategise about people Nikolic should meet at the upcoming Doha conference.
Nikolic replied about an hour later, delayed by a flight, saying there were 'not many interesting people' at the event. Epstein responded that Nikolic was 'the most interesting person there', adding: 'john sununu, has good stories.'
The Sununu campaign has disputed the mention, calling it 'a complete fabrication by someone proven to be a compulsive liar' and insisting 'neither John nor his father ever met or communicated in any way with Boris Nikolic or Jeffrey Epstein'.
As the Keene Sentinel has noted, it remains unclear whether the email refers to the candidate or his father, former Governor John H Sununu.
The controversy escalated in July 2026 after Sununu's campaign clarified his earlier denial of ever visiting Doha, following images produced by the Keene Sentinel placing him at the 2010 World Economic Forum summit referenced in the exchange.
Separately, travel records show Sununu visited Doha from 7 to 12 April 2001 with a congressional delegation that met Qatari royal and future prime minister Hamad bin Jasem. Together, the 2001 and 2010 visits undercut Sununu's on-camera claim that he had never been to Qatar.
Brown's allies seized on the issue during the primary. A $130,000 mailer funded by a pro-Brown political action committee showed a screenshot of the email and asked voters: 'Why would a Sununu show up in the files...?' Brown told the outlet he 'had nothing to do with' the mailer, but Sununu still beat him by more than 40 points.
The Fight for November
The Epstein reference has not stayed confined to the Republican primary. Democratic California Representative Ro Khanna used a July visit to New Hampshire to call on Sununu to 'come clean' about questions surrounding the Epstein email, according to Granite Post News, signalling the issue will likely feature in Democratic attacks through November.
Pappas has pivoted towards the general election, attacking Sununu in mid-August and asking voters at his primary-night event whether they are living in Trump's 'golden age'.
Republicans have countered through One Nation, a conservative group aligned with the Senate Leadership Fund, which launched adverts attacking Pappas over his 2021 vote for a sweeping climate and social-spending measure.
New Hampshire has not elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, but Granite State voters have shown a willingness to split tickets.
With control of the Senate potentially hanging on a handful of races, both campaigns have substantial financial resources ahead of 3 November. Neither Sununu nor his father has been shown, through any document made public so far, to have met or corresponded with Epstein, but the four words in a 2010 email remain a political issue for the candidate.

sources.news_title: Sununu to face Pappas in New Hampshire Senate race
sources.text:
CONCORD, N.H. — Republican John E. Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas will compete for an open U.S. Senate seat in New Hampshire in a race that has emerged as one of a handful around the country that could determine control of the chamber in November.
Sununu, a former U.S. senator, and Pappas, a member of the U.S. House, are vying to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision not to seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races. Both entered their respective party primaries as strong front-runners and now have just eight weeks to make their case to general election voters.
Republicans view the seat as an opportunity to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a critical part of that effort.
In other top races, Stefany Shaheen, Shaheen's daughter, won a close primary and will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in the race to fill Pappas' open seat in the 1st Congressional District. The 2nd Congressional District will feature a matchup between U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat seeking her second term, and Republican Lily Tang Williams.
Pappas, who is giving up his seat in the 1st Congressional District after four terms, defeated four other candidates, including democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who had been gaining on him in recent weeks.
Speaking to supporters at his family's restaurant in Manchester, he quickly sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu even though Sununu called him "a loser" during the 2024 presidential campaign.
"While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters," said Pappas, whose campaign also quickly posted a negative ad on social media calling Sununu "a sequel we can't afford."
"We've got to turn the page on Donald Trump's reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy and on costs, and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past," he said at his victory party.
Sununu, who spent six years in the U.S. House and one term in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008, called Pappas a career politician who has held office for virtually his entire adult life.
"He's not an independent voice for New Hampshire," Sununu said at his victory party at a Manchester ski area. "Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire."
Sununu defeated seven other Republicans to win the primary, including former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, who accused him of coasting on his name. Sununu's father and younger brother are both former governors.
Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because "he never got traction back again." He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him.
"I think what he's done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what's going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he's got a more stable base," Loomis said.
Stefany Shaheen and Maura Sullivan were the leading candidates among seven seeking the Democratic nomination in the 1st District.
Shaheen is a former city councilor in Portsmouth. She founded a business to help people with chronic medical conditions after one of her daughters was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She also is part of a bio-tech initiative in New Hampshire to advance regenerative medicine.
Speaking to her supporters Tuesday night before the race was called, Shaheen said she was campaigning to "take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs, the skyrocketing costs families are facing in New Hampshire and across the country." But she also said running against the president wouldn't be enough, that she would give voters a reason to turn out for the general election.
"We can bring the real change that's needed, starting with healthcare, starting with Medicare for all," she said.
Sullivan is a retired Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Barack Obama. A vice chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, Sullivan ran for the 1st District seat in 2018, losing in an 11-candidate primary to Pappas in his first congressional bid.
Her campaign did not immediately return a call and email seeking a response after Shaheen won. Earlier in the night, Sullivan addressed her supporters and thanked them for their hard work during the campaign.
"What we are doing right now is send such an incredible message for change, and that politics as usual is not, is not going to get us where we need to go," she said.
On the Republican side, political newcomer DiLorenzo, who owns a chain of car dealerships and has been endorsed by Trump, won the Republican primary. He defeated three other candidates, including Hollie Noveletsky, a veteran and nurse practitioner who runs a steel fabrication company and ran for the same seat two years ago.
"Our campaign is about prosperity," DiLorenzo told supporters. "I believe that Washington, D.C., needs more pragmatic businesspeople."
In the 2nd District, first-term incumbent Goodlander overcame a primary challenge from Paige Beauchemin, a progressive state lawmaker and nurse. Tang Williams, who was the nominee two years ago and was making her third attempt at the seat, won the Republican primary.
In contrast to the all-Democratic congressional delegation, Republicans dominate state government.
Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte defeated two little-known opponents in her primary as she seeks a second two-year term. Cinde Warmington, a healthcare attorney, was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.
Voters also were nominating candidates for the entire state Legislature, where Republicans hold a roughly 40-vote majority in the 400-member House and outnumber Democrats in the Senate 16-8.
Accustomed to going first when it comes to presidential primaries, New Hampshire is among the last states to hold state-level primary elections. But legislation passed this year moves future state primaries to the second Tuesday in June.

U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) won the Democratic nomination on Tuesday to succeed three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, while former Sen. John Sununu captured the Republican nomination, setting up an open-seat general election critical to both parties’ hopes of running the Senate.

Sununu faced a challenge from former Massachusetts senator and Trump administration alum Scott Brown, but ultimately beat him 68.5% to 26.7%. Several other Republicans finished in the distant single digits.
New Hampshire has not elected a Republican senator since 2010, but August University of New Hampshire polling shows Sununu leading Pappas 45% to 43%.
“We’re taking nothing for granted, this is a purple state,” Pappas told MS NOW. “We’ve got a path to victory. But it’s going to be a tough race.”
Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the Granite State by just three points in 2024, with all 10 counties shifting right since 2020.

sources.text:
Pappas and Sununu prevail in NH primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate
Chris Pappas (left) and John Sununu (right) will face off in what promises to be a very expensive U.S. Senate race. (Left: Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu to be U.S. senator, after the two candidates prevailed in their respective primaries Tuesday.
The results, projected by the Associated Press shortly after 8 p.m., solidified what will likely be a bare-knuckled, expensive general election fight for the Senate seat, which is open after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement.
Polls suggest the contest between Pappas, the current representative for the 1st Congressional District, and Sununu could be close, and both candidates had been positioning themselves for the general election months before the primary. As the polling has tightened, the race has taken on increasing significance to Democrats’ chances to flip control of the U.S. Senate, with Pappas’s shrinking advantage drawing national attention.
In winning his primary, Sununu held off a challenge from Scott Brown, the former U.S. senator from Massachusetts who has since moved to New Hampshire, after Brown attempted to align himself with President Donald Trump and run to Sununu’s right. Trump ultimately endorsed Sununu in February, spurning Brown and propelling Sununu into a lead Brown could never overcome.
Pappas, meanwhile, bested Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist from Exeter and first-time candidate who ran as a progressive. Manzur called for universal health care and attacked Pappas for his prior support of Israel; Pappas has since told the Bulletin he wanted “a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
In a statement after his victory, Sununu signaled awareness that the general election fight would be centered on the cost of living.
“We will keep listening, keep working, and stay laser-focused on the economy, jobs, and making life more affordable,” Sununu said in the statement.
“We will clean up Washington and hold politicians in both parties accountable,” Sununu continued. “I’ll push term limits, make Congress pay for the full cost of their healthcare, and cut Congress’ pay if they vote to shut down the government.”
Pappas had a similar message. “Everywhere I go, I hear the same thing: Life is too damn expensive,” he said in a victory speech Tuesday night, citing U.S.-led tariffs affecting businesses, the reduction of healthcare subsidies, and high gas and grocery prices.
“Donald Trump thinks all of this is just a hoax. In fact, he says we’re living in a golden age,” Pappas said. “Well, I think he’s living on another planet because does this feel like a golden age to you?”
Both candidates had decisive victories: Just before 9 p.m., Pappas commanded 62.5% of the vote compared to Manzur’s 35.4%; around the same time, Sununu had taken 69.1% of the vote compared to Brown’s 25.6%, according to the Associated Press.

Tuesday night’s Democratic primaries in New Hampshire delivered mixed results for candidates who made attacks on Israel a centerpiece of their closing arguments.
Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) trounced progressive activist Karishma Manzur by nearly a 2-to-1 margin (65%-33%) in the Senate primary, after Manzur attacked Pappas for his stance on Israel and called him a “shill for AIPAC” as a central message of her campaign.
Pappas is now facing a competitive general election against former Sen. John Sununu (R-NH), who is running to rejoin the Senate after nearly two decades out of office. Sununu is expected to be a formidable challenger who holds a narrow lead over Pappas in recent public polling.
The Cook Political Report rates the race as “Lean Democratic.” A longtime New Hampshire pollster told JI last week that Sununu is the underdog but is a strong and experienced candidate, and has a well-known and popular family name in the state, with a record of support from moderates and independents whom Pappas has previously worked to attract.
Pappas will likely be buoyed, however, by the strong national environment for Democrats, while Sununu will need to hold together a coalition of moderates skeptical of President Donald Trump and MAGA diehards in the GOP base.
Meanwhile, Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), narrowly beat military veteran and second-time candidate Maura Sullivan. Shaheen closed out the race with claims that AIPAC, which did not endorse and was not involved in either race, had been bundling contributions for Sullivan.
Shaheen’s advantage is partly attributable to her family name — but Sullivan came close to overcoming that advantage despite starting the race trailing Shaheen by double digits.
Shaheen went on air in the closing days of the race with ads accusing Sullivan of being “bankrolled” by AIPAC, and leaned into her opposition to Israel in interviews. Sullivan hit back in her own ad saying she doesn’t take any money from AIPAC.
Under pressure from the left in the wake of the war in Gaza, both Pappas and Sullivan recalibrated their stances on Israel during their primary races. Pappas, a pro-Israel moderate for most of his time in the House, backed away from his previous relationship with AIPAC and called for a “reset” of the U.S.-Israel relationship while voting “present” on an amendment to strip aid from Israel.
Democratic Majority for Israel and the Jewish Democratic Council of America congratulated Pappas on his victory.
Sullivan, who rejected efforts to cut aid to Israel earlier in the race, came around to supporting the suspension of at least some weapons sales to Israel.

Winners and losers from Tuesday's NH primary election
sources.text:
Republican John E. Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas will compete for an open U.S. Senate seat in New Hampshire in a race that has emerged as one of a handful around the country that could determine control of the chamber in November.
Sununu, a former U.S. senator, and Pappas, a member of the U.S. House, are vying to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision not to seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races. Both entered their respective party primaries as strong front-runners and now have just eight weeks to make their case to general election voters.

Republicans view the seat as an opportunity to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a critical part of that effort.
In other top races, Stefany Shaheen, Shaheen's daughter, won a close primary and will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in the race to fill Pappas' open seat in the 1st Congressional District. The 2nd Congressional District will feature a matchup between U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat seeking her second term, and Republican Lily Tang Williams.
Familiar names will compete in November for open Senate seat
Local
In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area.
Pappas, who is giving up his seat in the 1st Congressional District after four terms, defeated four other candidates, including democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who had been gaining on him in recent weeks.
Speaking to supporters at his family's restaurant in Manchester, he quickly sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu even though Sununu called him “a loser” during the 2024 presidential campaign.
“While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters,” said Pappas, whose campaign also quickly posted a negative ad on social media calling Sununu “a sequel we can't afford.”
“We've got to turn the page on Donald Trump's reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy and on costs, and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past," he said at his victory party.
Sununu, who spent six years in the U.S. House and one term in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008, called Pappas a career politician who has held office for virtually his entire adult life.
“He’s not an independent voice for New Hampshire,” Sununu said at his victory party at a Manchester ski area. “Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire.”
Sununu defeated seven other Republicans to win the primary, including former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, who accused him of coasting on his name. Sununu's father and younger brother are both former governors.
Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because “he never got traction back again.” He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him.
“I think what he’s done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what’s going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he’s got a more stable base,” Loomis said.
Senator's daughter survives tight contest for 1st District nomination
Stefany Shaheen and Maura Sullivan were the leading candidates among seven seeking the Democratic nomination in the 1st District.
Shaheen is a former city councilor in Portsmouth. She founded a business to help people with chronic medical conditions after one of her daughters was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She also is part of a bio-tech initiative in New Hampshire to advance regenerative medicine.
Speaking to her supporters Tuesday night before the race was called, Shaheen said she was campaigning to “take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs, the skyrocketing costs families are facing in New Hampshire and across the country.” But she also said running against the president wouldn’t be enough, that she would give voters a reason to turn out for the general election.
“We can bring the real change that’s needed, starting with healthcare, starting with Medicare for all,” she said.
Sullivan is a retired Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Barack Obama. A vice chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, Sullivan ran for the 1st District seat in 2018, losing in an 11-candidate primary to Pappas in his first congressional bid.
Her campaign did not immediately return a call and email seeking a response after Shaheen won. Earlier in the night, Sullivan addressed her supporters and thanked them for their hard work during the campaign.
"What we are doing right now is send such an incredible message for change, and that politics as usual is not, is not going to get us where we need to go," she said.
On the Republican side, political newcomer DiLorenzo, who owns a chain of car dealerships and has been endorsed by Trump, won the Republican primary. He defeated three other candidates, including Hollie Noveletsky, a veteran and nurse practitioner who runs a steel fabrication company and ran for the same seat two years ago.
“Our campaign is about prosperity,” DiLorenzo told supporters. “I believe that Washington, D.C., needs more pragmatic businesspeople.”
In the 2nd District, first-term incumbent Goodlander overcame a primary challenge from Paige Beauchemin, a progressive state lawmaker and nurse. Tang Williams, who was the nominee two years ago and was making her third attempt at the seat, won the Republican primary.
Incumbent Ayotte defeats 2 challengers in GOP primary for governor
In contrast to the all-Democratic congressional delegation, Republicans dominate state government.
Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte defeated two little-known opponents in her primary as she seeks a second two-year term. Cinde Warmington, a healthcare attorney, was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.
Voters also were nominating candidates for the entire state Legislature, where Republicans hold a roughly 40-vote majority in the 400-member House and outnumber Democrats in the Senate 16-8.
Accustomed to going first when it comes to presidential primaries, New Hampshire is among the last states to hold state-level primary elections. But legislation passed this year moves future state primaries to the second Tuesday in June.

sources.news_title: Pappas Powers Past Manzur, but Primary Leaves Dems Divided
sources.text:
New Hampshire Democrats avoided the sort of socialist-candidate shocker that’s shaken Senate races in Michigan and Florida, but the party is far from unified after Chris Pappas’ win Tuesday night.
After losing to the four-term congressman 65-33 percent, first-time candidate Karishma Manzur declined to endorse Pappas in the general election. Instead, she told supporters it was up to Pappas to earn their support.
“We cannot let John Sununu win in November, and we cannot empower Donald Trump. The majority is too important,” Manzur said Tuesday night. “In order for Chris Pappas to win this seat, he must win the support of the voters who chose our campaign tonight.
“When I speak to him shortly, I plan to congratulate him on his victory and discuss how he can earn our vote.”
That was not the expected trajectory of this race when Manzur, a medical scientist and Democratic Socialist, threw her hat in the ring. She had no name ID and few resources, spending just over $300,000 while Pappas spent more than $11 million. But her message resonated. In fact, she received a higher share of her party’s vote (32 percent) than former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown received from his (26 percent).
Manzur cast herself as the “real Democrat,” backing Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, and higher taxes on corporations and wealthy Americans. Pappas described himself as a pragmatic “New Hampshire Democrat” with a record of winning competitive elections.
Manzur made Israel and the influence of pro-Israel campaign donors defining issues in the race, accusing Pappas of accepting AIPAC-linked money and supporting weapons transfers that she said fueled a “genocide” in Gaza. The pressure coincided with Pappas distancing himself from his previous pro-Israel posture, including voting “present” on a proposal to end U.S. aid to Israel and declaring that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “has got to go.” Manzur invoked Netanyahu 10 times during last week’s WMUR debate, even in answers about housing and border security.
While her 32-point loss was larger than UNH Survey Center data predicted, her performance was strong enough to give her influence. Pappas tacitly acknowledged that fact in his remarks Tuesday night.
“I want to say something to everyone who supported another candidate in today’s primary, whether you voted for Karishma Manzur, Scott Brown, or someone else,” Pappas said. “I’m running to represent all Granite Staters, and this campaign is for you. The challenges that we face, after all, affect each and every one of us.”
Will it work? New Hampshire Democrats need it to.
“Chris Pappas added to his formidable history of wins. But having to scramble these final two weeks to shore up his left flank and still conceding over a third of the vote to an unknown DSA radical is less than ideal,” one campaign operative told NHJournal on background. “It suggests he won’t only have John Sununu to contend with this fall, but the base of an increasingly cranky party looking for their own AOC.”
Pappas turned his fire on a target that has already united many Democrats: President Donald Trump.
“Donald Trump says we’re living in a golden age. Well, I think he’s living on another planet. Does this feel like a golden age to you? It might be a golden age if you’re a member of the Epstein class. It might be a golden age if you’re a contributor to the new ballroom, buying special treatment,” Pappas said.
“It might be a golden age if you’re Donald Trump, the president of the United States, because we’ve got a leader who thinks the rules don’t apply to him.”
Pappas linked Sununu to Trump, claiming his GOP opponent “Supported Trump’s tax breaks for the ultra-wealthy on the backs of hardworking families that added trillions of dollars to our debt. Sununu was a cheerleader for Trump’s war in Iran, just like he was for the war in Iraq, which has sent gas over $4 a gallon.”
In his victory speech, Sununu hit Pappas as “ineffective, partisan, and out of touch with New Hampshire.”

sources.news_title: Chris Pappas projected to win New Hampshire Democratic nomination to the US Senate
sources.text:
US Rep. Chris Pappas swiftly defeated progressive opponent Karishma Manzur in a Democratic Senate primary in New Hampshire on Tuesday, capping off one of several races in which criticism of Israel and AIPAC became prominent talking points.
The Associated Press called the race just an hour after polls closed, at 6 p.m., when 22% of the votes had been counted. As the night wore on, with 88% of the votes tallied, Pappas had accrued 65% of the votes to Manzur’s 32.8%.
'We’ve got to turn the page on Donald Trump’s reckless leadership'
Israel featured heavily in the race, with both Pappas and Manzur attacking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Pappas, however, supports Israel’s right to security and condemned the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack on Israel, whereas Manzur questioned Israel’s right to respond to it.
“Today, the voters of New Hampshire have sent a clear message: They’re fed up with what’s happening in our politics, and they’re ready for change,” Pappas told supporters on Tuesday evening. “We’ve got to turn the page on [US President] Donald Trump’s reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy.”
Having secured the Democratic nomination, Pappas is seeking to fill the seat of three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is not seeking reelection this year. As he and Manzur spoke to the press during the final weeks of the campaign, their messaging often included condemnations of Israeli leadership.
New Hampshire Democrats chose Pappas, a four-term congressman, as their Senate nominee at a time when their party is hoping to take control of both houses of Congress. Their selection of Pappas, seen as the establishment candidate, could play a pivotal role in November, in a swing state where many voters still split tickets.
Pappas will face former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement, in the general election. Sununu served one term in the Senate, from 2003 to 2009, immediately following three terms in the US House.
Two other Democratic primaries, for neighboring US House seats, likewise focused outsized attention on Israel in recent weeks. But one of the races featured a decisive victory on Tuesday, while in the other there was a very narrow margin between the two candidates.
The AP declared Goodlander as the projected winner an hour after polls closed
US Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat from New Hampshire, enters the US Capitol on August 31, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a one-term incumbent, trounced progressive state lawmaker Paige Beauchemin in the 2nd Congressional District, which includes New Hampshire’s capital, Concord, and the city of Nashua. The AP declared Goodlander the projected winner an hour after polls closed. Later in the night, with 84% of the votes tallied, Goodlander had 81.5% to Beauchemin’s 18.3%.
In the next-door Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District, City Councilor Stefany Shaheen narrowly defeated former US Marine Capt. Maura Sullivan in a contest that included numerous other candidates. According to the Associated Press, Shaheen had 37.3% of the votes compared to Sullivan’s 35%, with 91% of the ballots tallied.
The winner of that race will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo, an automotive executive who has Trump’s support, in the November election.
Shaheen is a healthcare advocate and daughter of Jeanne Shaheen, whose Senate seat Pappas is hoping to secure in November. Her opponent, Sullivan, served as the assistant secretary for Veterans Affairs in the Obama administration.
Similar to the US Senate primary hopefuls, candidates in these two races seemed to share near-unanimous disdain for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. They, too, had a spectrum of opinions on the Jewish state, with moderates asserting Israel’s right to defend itself and progressives placing most of the blame for the Gaza war on Israel.
The candidates in the US House races also spent significant airtime in recent weeks blasting the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group. AIPAC has rejected comparisons to corporate PACs, noting that it is membership-driven, and claims to be transparent about its funds.
Both Shaheen and Beauchemin accused their opponents of taking AIPAC funds, simply because donors who contributed to the lobby also gave to their campaigns. Sullivan and Goodlander denied these allegations, maintaining that they took no money from AIPAC.

sources.text:
Pappas and Sununu to face off in November for New Hampshire Senate seat
Former Sen. John Sununu will face Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire's Senate race in November. The race is one of the most competitive in the midterms and could help determine control of the Senate.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
One of the most competitive midterm Senate races has its matchup set for November. Former U.S. Senator John Sununu won the Republican primary in New Hampshire last night. He will face Congressman Chris Pappas, who won the Democratic primary. That's according to race calls by The Associated Press. They're running to replace Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in a race that both parties see as key to determining control of the Senate. Josh Rogers with New Hampshire Public Radio is up early for us after a late night, and he's with us now to tell us what happened. Good morning, Josh.
JOSH ROGERS, BYLINE: Good morning, Michel.
MARTIN: So walk us through the key results.
ROGERS: Well, there was a tight open Democratic primary for one of the state's two House seats that was really only called early this morning. And that was for Stefany Shaheen. She's the daughter of Jeanne Shaheen. That was a big race. The younger Shaheen beat former Obama administration official Maura Sullivan. The race featured millions of dollars of outside spending and really became quite nasty and personal. That was by far the tightest primary.
But the Senate race is the bigger deal. It's also an open-seat race due to Jeanne Shaheen's retirement. Democrats chose four-term Congressman Chris Pappas, a political moderate, over a more progressive challenger, Karishma Manzur. And Republicans chose John E. Sununu over former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown. Sununu comes from a big political family here and actually held the same seat he's now seeking nearly 20 years ago.
MARTIN: And President Trump had backed Sununu over Brown. But given Trump's low approval ratings, does that actually help him now? Or would it be better for Sununu...
ROGERS: Well...
MARTIN: ...To maybe keep some distance from the president going forward?
ROGERS: I mean, we'll see if it helps. It may have helped him in the primary, but the distance-making on Sununu's part is already happening. During the primary, Sununu tended to downplay the significance of Trump's endorsement, and he's also worked to distance himself from the president on some key issues. He said he never would have attacked Iran, for instance, and he's criticized Trump's tariff policies. But Trump made the endorsement. Sununu accepted it. And Chris Pappas is going to and has been looking to tie Sununu to Trump really at every turn.
And, you know, for Sununu, Trump's backing does mean money and support from the party's base. And for Trump, you know, picking Sununu gives him a better chance of flipping a seat that a Democrat, Jeanne Shaheen, has held since she beat Sununu back in 2008. So we'll see.
MARTIN: And what about the issues? What issues have New Hampshire voters been telling you are most important to them?
ROGERS: They've been talking a lot about the economy - really the high costs across the board, from gasoline to healthcare and housing. The war in Iran is another big concern. So are tariffs. Canada is a major trading partner with New Hampshire, and state tourism officials have reported that cross-border visits from Canadian tourists were down significantly this summer. So tariffs are really a concern here.
MARTIN: And, you know - and the Trump administration sent election observers to New Hampshire and other states for primary elections. What were they doing yesterday? And what do local officials think about them being there?
ROGERS: Well, local officials have said nondisruptive monitoring is fine. And from what I understand, that's basically what took place here in New Hampshire yesterday. In the run-up to this election, there was real concern that it wasn't going to be noninvasive monitoring. And there's been tension between state election officials and the Trump administration over things like nonpublic voter rolls, and the possibility of more intense monitoring in November remains a real concern. And - you know, and it obviously comes as President Trump continues to allege without evidence that election tampering is widespread in New Hampshire and across the country.
MARTIN: That's New Hampshire Public Radio's Josh Rogers. Josh, thank you.
ROGERS: You're welcome.

Few Surprises In Midterm 2026 Primary: Pappas, Sununu Advance To Senate Race; Goodlander Fends Off Challenge
Update: DiLorenzo, Tang Williams win GOP nominations. Shaheen wins 1st Congressional District Democratic primary; an easy win for Ayotte.
CONCORD, NH — There were few surprises on Tuesday as voters went to the polls to nominate gubernatorial, Senate, Congressional, and other candidates in New Hampshire.
In the governor’s race, incumbent Republican Kelly Ayotte easily fended off challenges from Shaun Fife and Bob Wayne McClory with nearly 91 percent of the vote. She will face Democratic nominee Cinde Warmington, who was unopposed, in November.
Former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu bested former Sen. Scott Brown by more than 40 points to win the Republican nomination for the seat being vacated by U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who beat Sununu in 2008. U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas easily beat a challenge from his left, Karishma Manzur, by about 31,000 votes. Manzur, a scientist and peace activist, had shown poll movement toward the end of the campaign. She beat Pappas in Keene and Plymouth as well as two wards in Concord.
Find out what's happening in Concordfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
Anthony DiLorenzo, the owner of the Key Auto Group, won the Republican nomination for the open 1st Congressional District seat vacated by Pappas. Hollie Noveletsky, who placed second two years ago, placed second again this year, earning about 26 percent of the vote.
The 1st Congressional District primary was a nail-biter all evening, but around 12:30 a.m., with about 90 percent of the vote counted, Stefany Shaheen was declared the winner, with a 1,600-vote lead over Maura Sullivan, who placed second in the 2018 open-seat race. Carleigh Beriont trailed with 22 percent of the vote. Shaheen showed solid numbers across most of the Seacoast while Sullivan led in most of the district’s western communities, including Manchester. She also led Shaheen by 100 votes in her home city of Portsmouth with 90 percent of the votes counted.
Find out what's happening in Concordfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
Beriont, a member of the board of selectmen in Hampton, was originally reported by AP as only receiving around 5 percent of the vote in her hometown.
According to revised data, she actually won Hampton with more than 800 votes. She also won in Newmarket and Tamworth.
In the 2nd Congressional District, it will be a rematch of 2024, with now-incumbent U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander facing a challenge from Lily Tang Williams. Goodlander was able to beat a challenge from her left, besting state Rep. Paige Beauchemin by more than 60 percent. Williams won the nomination with nearly 65 percent of the vote against three other Republicans, Victor Orlando, Dan Nicholson, and Michael Anthony Callis.
2026 Candidate, Campaign Responses
Warmington’s campaign manager, Andrea Cervone, called the Democratic nominee a champion for working families who would focus on building a New Hampshire where everyone can afford a home.
“Right now,” she said, “too many Granite Staters are struggling to make ends meet in the Trump-Ayotte economy — from soaring property taxes and grocery bills to skyrocketing health care premiums and electric rates. This November, voters in every corner of the state will turn the page on Kelly Ayotte’s failed record of soaring costs and caving to Donald Trump by electing a proven leader who puts working people first.”
Sullivan said Wednesday morning she knew the race would not be easy, but she loved New Hampshire and its communities, seeing all their strength and goodness. She also congratulated Shaheen.
“I also want to say a huge thank you to the hundreds of volunteers and local leaders who endorsed our campaign, hosted house parties, knocked on doors, made phone calls, chipped in 5 dollars, baked a dessert for a canvas kick-off, or held a sign,” she said. “You believed in change, in hope, in service, and that even in these dark times in our country, politics could be fun, and even joyful again. I will always be incredibly grateful for your trust and support. I want to thank my incredible team. I couldn’t be more proud of the movement for change that we (built) together from the ground up. Your commitment to fighting day in and day out for this beloved country of ours will forever inspire me.”
Goodlander, who celebrated her victory at Feathered Friend Brewing in Concord, thanked election officials, volunteers, and town clerks who worked hard to ensure voting went off without a hitch.
“Running for office is never easy,” she said. “It means asking your neighbors for the most precious thing that they could really ever give you: their trust. But the willingness to step forward is what democracy is all about, and I want to thank you above all for every person who put their name on the ballot today.”
Tang Williams, who fled communist China during the Mao revolution, said the victory belonged not to her but to Granite Staters who believe in the American Dream.
“I’ll work for every Granite Stater as an independent voice — not the extremists driving today’s Democrat Party,” she said, after having a private party at her home in Weare. “Maggie Goodlander has had two years in Congress. Now she has to answer for what she has, and hasn’t, accomplished. I’m ready to fight to make New Hampshire affordable again and preserve the American Dream.”
Scott Maltzie, the chairman of the NH GOP, congratulated Ayotte, Sununu, DiLorenzo, and Tang Williams.
“Governor Ayotte has delivered for all of New Hampshire and kept our state moving in the right direction,” he said. “Opioid Lobbyist Cinde Warmington has spent her career putting her self-interest ahead of what was best for New Hampshire. From lying on behalf of Purdue Pharma to advocating for a notorious pill mill, Cinde Warmington has made it clear that she will put herself ahead of us every chance she gets. Voters will reject the Opioid Lobbyist this November.”
Sununu, he said, was “exactly the candidate” Republicans needed to take on Pappas.
“Chris Pappas is a do-nothing politician looking for a six-year promotion after spending the last seven years in Congress with little to show for it,” Maltzie said. “Granite Staters deserve a Senator who will put New Hampshire first, deliver results, and bring the New Hampshire Advantage to Washington. John E. Sununu has the experience and determination to get the job done, and I look forward to working with him to defeat Chris Pappas and send him packing in November.”
DiLorenzo, he said, was a true Granite Stater with business experience, who built his career on hard work and perseverance. Tang Williams, Maltzie said, was “a fearless fighter” who shows up, talks to voters, and holds town halls, unlike Goodlander, “who only seems to show up in New Hampshire when it is time to campaign.”
Ken Martin, the chairman of the Democratic National Committee, congratulated Pappas, saying he had learned the value of hard work by helping to run his family’s small business.
“Democrats have chosen a proven leader who knows how to deliver for working families,” he said. “In the Senate, Chris will lower costs, protect healthcare, make housing more affordable, create good-paying jobs, support small businesses, and invest in communities throughout New Hampshire. With Democrats united, the DNC is ready to work alongside Chris to protect this seat and deliver for families across the Granite State.”
Martin also congratulated Warmington for being the party’s nominee, calling her a fighter for New Hampshire who has a track record of standing up for working families.
“While Kelly Ayotte has turned her back on New Hampshire families, Cinde will be a governor who lowers costs, makes healthcare and housing more affordable, supports small businesses, and invests in public education,” he said. “The DNC is ready to help organize and mobilize voters to elect candidates like Cinde who put Granite Staters first.”
The Senate Majority PAC also congratulated Pappas, calling him a fighter who had taken own President Donald Trump’s “reckless tariffs” and standing against the war in Iran.
“The contrast with John E. Sununu could not be clearer,” Lauren French, the org’s spokeswoman, said. “Sununu cashed in with the same corporate interests he sold New Hampshire out to nearly two decades ago. He has no plan to lower costs, no interest in fighting corruption, and no willingness to stand up to Donald Trump. He isn’t running to change anything. He's running for his next paycheck.”
The Republican Governors Association also congratulated Ayotte for winning the nomination and tackling the state’s housing shortage, strengthening public safety, and protecting the New Hampshire Advantage.
“Ayotte has kept her promise of no income or sales tax, while keeping New Hampshire on the right track,” RGA Chairman Governor Greg Gianforte said. “The contrast couldn’t be clearer: Cinde Warmington cashed checks lobbying for Purdue Pharma, called OxyContin a ‘miracle drug,’ and wants to turn New Hampshire into Massachusetts. Warmington will sell out New Hampshire while Kelly Ayotte will continue to lead with common sense.”
Outgoing U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen congratulated her daughter, Pappas, and Goodlander in an email about 30 minutes before the race was called for her daughter.
“Billy and I are enormously proud that Stefany answered the call to serve the community she was born and raised in,” she said. “In New Hampshire’s first district, Stefany has sent her own children to our schools, started a business, served on the Portsmouth City Council and police commission, and advocated for affordable health care and clean water. She has worked tirelessly over the last year to earn voters’ support — and I have no doubt that she’ll be the champion working families need in Congress.”
Other Races
In the Executive Council races,
Tobin Menard beat Kim Strathdee for the Republican nomination in District 2 with about 55 percent of the vote reported. He will face off against incumbent Karen Liot Hill.
In District 3, incumbent Janet Stevens easily beat Gregory Whirley by a two-to-one margin.
Incumbent John Stephen, in District 4, was also successful, receiving more than 77 percent of the vote against Terese Bastarache and Harriet Cady.
With 92 percent reporting, Meg Hagaman has a 6,000-vote lead over Sarah Rogers in the Merrimack County Attorney GOP primary. Jon Raiche is a distant third. She will face Steven Endres in the final.
Frank Cassidy will be the Republican nominee for sheriff in Merrimack County after defeating Jason Gerhard and Ben Weir by wide margins. Peter Shephard, the Democrat, ran unopposed.
Kathleen Donnelly easily bested Dianne Schuett in the Democrat Merrimack County Treasurer primary.
Jon Stark won the Register of Probate GOP primary in Rockingham County with two-thirds of the vote against Shawn Faber.
Chuck Massahos, the incumbent GOP sheriff of Rockingham County, beat Paul Bean, with nearly 80 percent of the vote.

sources.text:
Greek-American Chris Pappas Wins Democratic Senate Primary in New Hampshire, Will Face John Sununu
CONCORD, N.H. – Greek-American Democrat Chris Pappas won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire on Tuesday, defeating four other candidates and setting up a November showdown with Republican John E. Sununu for an open Senate seat that has emerged as one of a handful around the country that could determine control of the chamber.
Pappas, a four-term member of the U.S. House, and Sununu, a former U.S. senator, are vying to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision not to seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races. Both entered their respective party primaries as strong front-runners and now have just eight weeks to make their case to general election voters.
Pappas, who is giving up his seat in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District after four terms, defeated four other candidates, including democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who had been gaining on him in recent weeks.
Republicans view the Senate seat as an opportunity to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a critical part of that effort.
Speaking to supporters at his family’s restaurant in Manchester, Pappas quickly sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu even though Sununu called Trump “a loser” during the 2024 presidential campaign.
“While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters,” said Pappas, whose campaign also quickly posted a negative ad on social media calling Sununu “a sequel we can’t afford.”
“We’ve got to turn the page on Donald Trump’s reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy and on costs, and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past,” Pappas said at his victory party.
Sununu, who spent six years in the U.S. House and one term in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008, called Pappas a career politician who has held office for virtually his entire adult life.
“He’s not an independent voice for New Hampshire,” Sununu said at his victory party at a Manchester ski area. “Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire.”
Sununu defeated seven other Republicans to win the primary, including former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, who accused him of coasting on his name. Sununu’s father and younger brother are both former governors.
Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because “he never got traction back again.” He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him.
“I think what he’s done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what’s going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he’s got a more stable base,” Loomis said.
Democrats in Tight Contest for 1st District Nomination
Still outstanding were the results in the Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District, where the candidates included Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, and retired Marine Maura Sullivan.
Shaheen and Sullivan were the leading candidates among seven seeking the Democratic nomination in the 1st District.
Shaheen is a former city councilor in Portsmouth. She founded a business to help people with chronic medical conditions after one of her daughters was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She also is part of a biotech initiative in New Hampshire to advance regenerative medicine.
Sullivan is a retired Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Barack Obama. A vice chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, Sullivan ran for the 1st District seat in 2018, losing in an 11-candidate primary to Pappas in his first congressional bid.
On the Republican side, political newcomer Anthony DiLorenzo, who owns a chain of car dealerships and has been endorsed by Trump, won the Republican primary. He defeated three other candidates, including Hollie Noveletsky, a veteran and nurse practitioner who runs a steel fabrication company and ran for the same seat two years ago.
In the 2nd District, first-term incumbent Maggie Goodlander overcame a primary challenge from Paige Beauchemin, a progressive state lawmaker and nurse. Lily Tang Williams, who was the Republican nominee two years ago and was making her third attempt at the seat, won the GOP primary.
Incumbent Ayotte Defeats Two Challengers in GOP Primary for Governor
In contrast to the all-Democratic congressional delegation, Republicans dominate state government.
Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte defeated two little-known opponents in her primary as she seeks a second two-year term. Cinde Warmington, a healthcare attorney, was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.
Voters also were nominating candidates for the entire state Legislature, where Republicans hold a roughly 40-vote majority in the 400-member House and outnumber Democrats in the Senate 16-8.
Accustomed to going first when it comes to presidential primaries, New Hampshire is among the last states to hold state-level primary elections. But legislation passed this year moves future state primaries to the second Tuesday in June.
The November Senate contest between Pappas and Sununu is expected to draw national attention as both parties fight for control of the chamber. For the Greek-American community, the race also places Pappas, one of New Hampshire’s prominent Greek-American political figures, at the center of a closely watched campaign with national implications.

New Hampshire Senate Primary: Sununu beats Brown, Pappas beats Manzur

New Hampshire Senate Primary: Sununu beats Brown, Pappas beats Manzur
New Hampshire voters had their say, and front-runners for the Senate race from both parties emerged successful.
Retiring Senator Jeanne Shaheen left her Senate seat wide-open in one fo the most-watched races of this election cycle. Decision Desk HQ and The Associated Press called the race winners on Tuesday night.
In the Republican primary, former Senator John E. Sununu defeated Scott Brown by a wide margin, and on the Democratic side, Rep. Chris Pappas defeated scientist and first-time progressive candidate Karishma Manzur, who earned 34% of the vote to Pappas's 64 percent with just over 50% of the votes counted.
Senate GOP primary: Sununu vs. Brown
The Sununu family has long been popular in New Hampshire: the candidate's father John H. Sununu and brother Chris Sununu served three and four terms as governor respectively. Even before Trump endorsed him, John E. Sununu was leading Brown in the polls by double digits.
He also raised more money: over $4 million for this race, while Brown raised about $2.1 million, according to FEC filings.
And Sununu has won this seat before, defeating then-Gov. Jeanne Shaheen in 2002 to serve one term before Shaheen defeated him in 2008.
Brown, on the other hand, served as senator in Massachusetts through special election from 2010 to 2013, before moving to New Hampshire and making an unsuccessful bid for senate in the state in 2014.
Senate Democratic primary: Pappas vs. Manzur
In the Democratic race, Pappas, who is known to be a more moderate candidate, won despite the enthusiasm progressives are receiving all across the country.
Pappas led by double digits in the polls, but recently, Manzur, a scientist, gained. In the August UNH poll, she had cut Pappas’s lead in half, and his lead dropped by 10 points in the Saint Anselm poll. With her support from progressives and young people, her momentum seemed to mirror races around the country, where anti-establishment, more progressive candidates are capitalizing on voters’ frustrations with their party’s approach to dealing with the Trump administration.
In fact, Pappas has broken with his party in the past, including his support for the Laken Riley act last year, a controversial immigration bill which critics say gives excessive power to state attorney generals and ICE.
Both Sununu and Pappas were already taking jabs at each other despite not being in competition, which largely showed their confidence in winning the primaries. They will now face each other in the November general election.

sources.news_title: Pappas and Sununu prevail in primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate
sources.text:
Pappas and Sununu prevail in primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate
Chris Pappas (left) and John Sununu (right) will face off in what promises to be a very expensive U.S. Senate race. (Left: Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu to be U.S. senator, after the two candidates prevailed in their respective primaries Tuesday.
The results, projected by the Associated Press shortly after 8 p.m., solidified what will likely be a bare-knuckled, expensive general election fight for the Senate seat, which is open after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement.
Polls suggest the contest between Pappas, the current representative for the 1st Congressional District, and Sununu could be close, and both candidates had been positioning themselves for the general election months before the primary. As the polling has tightened, the race has taken on increasing significance to Democrats’ chances to flip control of the U.S. Senate, with Pappas’s shrinking advantage drawing national attention.
In winning his primary, Sununu held off a challenge from Scott Brown, the former U.S. senator from Massachusetts who has since moved to New Hampshire, after Brown attempted to align himself with President Donald Trump and run to Sununu’s right. Trump ultimately endorsed Sununu in February, spurning Brown and propelling Sununu into a lead Brown could never overcome.
Pappas, meanwhile, bested Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist from Exeter and first-time candidate who ran as a progressive. Manzur called for universal health care and attacked Pappas for his prior support of Israel; Pappas has since told the Bulletin he wanted “a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
In a statement after his victory, Sununu signaled awareness that the general election fight would be centered on the cost of living.
“We will keep listening, keep working, and stay laser-focused on the economy, jobs, and making life more affordable,” Sununu said in the statement.
“We will clean up Washington and hold politicians in both parties accountable,” Sununu continued. “I’ll push term limits, make Congress pay for the full cost of their healthcare, and cut Congress’ pay if they vote to shut down the government.”
Pappas had a similar message. “Everywhere I go, I hear the same thing: Life is too damn expensive,” he said in a victory speech Tuesday night, citing U.S.-led tariffs affecting businesses, the reduction of healthcare subsidies, and high gas and grocery prices.
“Donald Trump thinks all of this is just a hoax. In fact, he says we’re living in a golden age,” Pappas said. “Well, I think he’s living on another planet because does this feel like a golden age to you?”
Both candidates had decisive victories: Just before 9 p.m., Pappas commanded 62.5% of the vote compared to Manzur’s 35.4%; around the same time, Sununu had taken 69.1% of the vote compared to Brown’s 25.6%, according to the Associated Press.

sources.text:
(The Center Square) — Democratic New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas will face former Sen. John E. Sununu in the November elections to settle an open U.S. Senate race that could help decide the balance of power in Washington.
In Tuesday's primary elections, Pappas handily won the Democratic Party's nomination in a crowded four-way race for the seat being vacated by outgoing Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a three-term Democrat who is retiring.
With about 25% of the votes counted, Pappas had 62% of the vote when the Associated Press called the race in his favor shortly after 8 p.m., about an hour after the polls closed. Karishma Manzur, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had 36% of the vote, while several other Democratic contenders had less than single digits, according to the AP's unofficial tally.
Meanwhile, Sununu beat former Massachusetts U.S. Sen. Scott Brown in Tuesday's GOP primary to win the party's nomination, setting the stage for a showdown with Pappas in the general election. Sununu had nearly 70% of the vote to Brown's 25% when the AP called the race about an hour after the polls closed.
Sununu, a member of one of New Hampshire's most storied political families, was defeated by Shaheen in 2008. Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 until 2013, also lost a challenge to Shaheen in the 2014 Senate race.
Sununu's political comeback campaign has also been endorsed by second-term Republican President Donald Trump. He said the Senate race is one of several pivotal to keeping the GOP's majority in the midterms.
Flipping the Senate seat, held by Democrats since 2008, is a key goal for Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. The National Republican Senatorial Committee has listed the seat as a toss-up race, saying internal polling suggests that Republicans have a slight edge over Democrats. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the Senate race as "leaning Democrat."
Republicans have a 53-45 edge over Democrats in the U.S. Senate, with two independents caucusing with the minority party.
"After personally recruiting Sununu to run, Leader John Thune and Senate Republicans have expanded the map and are poised to flip the Granite State," Senate Leadership Fund Executive
Director Alex Latcham said in a statement. "From now until November, SLF will spend every day highlighting John E. Sununu's positive vision for New Hampshire while exposing the corruption, self-dealing, and radical record of Washington insider Chris Pappas."
New Hampshire Democratic Party Chairman Ray Buckley criticized Sununu for being Trump's "hand-picked" candidate "because he knows Sununu will be his pro-Trump puppet in the U.S. Senate."
"Maybe if Sununu hadn't become so out of touch from cashing in with corporate special interests and making millions, he might've realized that Granite Staters are fed up with Trump's war with Iran, toxic tariffs, and health care cuts that keep driving costs up," Buckley said. "While John Sununu's preoccupied with appeasing Donald Trump, Chris Pappas is focused on doing what's best for New Hampshire."
Further down Tuesday's ballot, Shaheen's daughter, Stefany, was still battling for votes in a Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District to replace Pappas against ex-Marine Maria Sullivan.
By 8:30 p.m. Shaheen was ahead with 36% of the vote to Sullivan's 34%, according to the AP, which hadn't yet called the race.
In the GOP primary for the 1st Congressional District, Trump-endorsed political newcomer Anthony DiLorenzo, who owns a chain of car dealerships and collision centers, defeated Hollie Noveletsky, an ironworks business owner, and Manchester state Rep. Brian Cole, according to the AP’s tally.
National Republicans have also made flipping New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District a top target this year. The National Republican Congressional Committee has pumped money and resources into the race and is expected to ramp up spending after the primary. Meanwhile, Democrats hope to defend the seat they have held since 2017 despite the district’s competitive landscape.
In other races, incumbent Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte easily won the party's nomination to run for another two-year term after fending off a challenge Tuesday from two GOP contenders.
Ayotte, a former U.S. senator first elected two years ago, will face Democrat Cinde Warmington, an attorney and former executive council member who was unopposed on Tuesday's ballot.

Chris Pappas wins NH Democratic Senate primary
Gay congressman running to succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
New Hampshire Congressman Chris Pappas on Tuesday won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in the U.S. Senate.
Pappas defeated Karishma Manzur, who was his primary challenger, by a 61.8-36.1 percent margin.
The gay congressman will face off against former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, who defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown in the Republican primary.
“Tonight’s victory sends a clear message that voters are looking for leaders who will fight for their rights, their freedoms, and to be treated with dignity and respect,” said Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson in a statement.
She campaigned for Pappas in Manchester, New Hampshire’s largest city, on Aug. 30.
“Chris Pappas has delivered results, stood up for equality, and showed up for the people he serves,” said Robinson in her statement. “HRC was proud to mobilize Equality Voters across New Hampshire to help power this win. We don’t have a second to waste between now and November. We look forward to continuing our work with Rep. Pappas as he drives toward victory in November so he can help return a pro-equality majority to the United States Senate.”
A poll the University of New Hampshire Survey Center released on Aug. 26 showed Sununu ahead of Pappas by a 45-43 percent margin if they were to face off in the general election. The margin of error is +/-2.1 percent.
Pappas would become the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate if he were to win in November.

Markey’s primary win deemed success for LGBTQ activists
Mass. lawmaker champions transgender rights
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) clinched the Democratic seat for his reelection campaign in Massachusetts’s primary election on Tuesday.
Markey won the deep-blue state with 64.8 percent of the vote, according to NBC News, triumphing over Marine Corps combat veteran and Congressman Seth Moulton, who received 35.2 percent of the vote.
Massachusetts’s primary election, which determined which Democratic candidate will head to the polls to face off against the Republican challenger in November, is being considered a victory for LGBTQ-inclusive policy, as well as for a divisive pro-transgender rights candidate — both things Markey has become an outspoken champion of.
Markey has experience at multiple levels of government, from the state level, where he served three terms in the state House of Representatives, to his federal tenure, including 20 terms in the U.S. House of Representatives and is now serving his second term as a senator. He has become a fixture of a changing Democratic Party in one of the most consistently blue places in the U.S.
This primary — and much of the national discussion surrounding the Senate seat — focused a lot of campaigning power on fighting the growing sentiment, led mostly by Republicans, that the frustration many Americans feel lends itself to an anti-establishment and anti-incumbent attitude.
Markey ran his campaign using his past as a reflection of his commitment to constantly putting his best foot forward for Bay Staters — particularly with apprehension for issues younger and more progressive democrats have been righting for — including Green New Deal and “Medicare for All” while Moulton — who was also elected to federal office prior to this run — campaigned on being younger than Markey, arguing that he was not the same type of established politician.
Moulton also faced backlash for negative comments about trans athletes, sparking criticism for those who did want younger candidate but want for trans rights to be protected.
Markey’s track record of supporting the LGBTQ community is one of the most clear in federal politics, one that has garnered a “100 percent lifetime voting record” on the Human Rights Campaign’s PAC politician review scorecard.
That list of Markey’s actions includes being a cosponsor of the Equality Act, driving landmark legislation to ensure federal protections for LGBTQ Americans, and being one of the most vocal proponents for trans rights in the federal government — specifically in multiple appropriations bills and in the National Defense Authorization Act. He was also the lead sponsor of the Transgender Health Care Access Act and the Transgender Bill of Rights resolution.
Markey first introduced the Transgender Bill of Rights in the Senate in 2023, where it ultimately failed to be brought to law. He reintroduced the legislation this year once again. This was a direct response to the attitude pushed by many conservatives after 2021, when the push to minimize trans rights started to become a key part of their cause and has been constantly propped up by the Trump-Vance administration.
“Massachusetts needs a senator who stands up and fights back, a senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey said during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”
Following the calling of the primary, a slew of LGBTQ organizations rallied behind Markey, many pushing his past as an asset that puts his money where his mouth is through advocating for legislation specifically protecting the LGBTQ community.
Tyler Hack, the executive director of the Christopher Street Project, an organization dedicated to pushing for legal protections for trans americans, released a statement following Markey’s win. Hack argued that putting forward such a staunchly pro-trans candidate is a win for the community, especially after endorsing him earlier this year.
“Tonight, anti-trans politics lost. Massachusetts rejected the idea that attacking transgender people is a shortcut to political power. Voters chose a different path: one where equality is not negotiable, cruelty is not courage, and transgender people do not have to disappear for Democrats to succeed.”
The Human Rights Campaign also endorsed him as a candidate earlier this year and issued a statement via its president, Kelley Robinson.
“Ed Markey has spent decades fighting for LGBTQ+ equality, for working people, and for a more livable world,” Robinson said. “He knows why equality matters. He’s stood with us no matter what. We were proud to endorse him this year, and when a pro-equality majority takes back the Senate this fall, we will continue to count on him as a champion for our community.”
Markey is running for reelection against Republican John Deaton in November, where he is expected to win.

As Washington shifts right, Democratic Socialists gain ground
Next major test for movement comes in Midwest
As President Donald Trump’s second administration has pushed the federal government further to the right on issues ranging from immigration to LGBTQ rights, a different political movement has been gaining momentum inside the Democratic Party.
From industrial communities in upstate New York to Colorado’s Front Range, candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have won a series of victories in Democratic primaries this year, in several cases defeating longtime incumbents who had represented Democratic strongholds for years. Their success has reignited debate over the Democratic Party’s future, as a growing faction of progressive voters calls for a more confrontational approach to economic inequality, healthcare, housing, labor rights, climate policy, and LGBTQ protections rather than what they view as the party’s increasingly cautious establishment.
These victories also reflect a broader ideological divergence in American politics. While Republicans under Trump have embraced a more conservative governing agenda, many Democratic primary voters in safely blue districts appear to be rewarding candidates running on unapologetically progressive platforms that reject incremental change in favor of more sweeping reforms.
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the nation’s largest socialist organization, says it has more than 100,000 members and chapters in all 50 states. The organization advocates what it describes as democratic socialism — promoting social and economic equality through democratic government while supporting a larger public role in healthcare, housing, labor protections, education, and other social programs alongside a regulated market economy.
On its website, the DSA explains its goals are to utilize “progressive movements for social change while establishing an openly democratic socialist presence in American communities and politics.”
For LGBTQ Americans, the organization has long supported expansive nondiscrimination protections, marriage equality, transgender rights, and broader legal protections through a platform first adopted in 2017. Its LGBTQ policy calls for federal legislation prohibiting discrimination, expanded access to gender-affirming healthcare, reproductive freedom, and opposition to laws targeting LGBTQ people.
The movement’s biggest victories came in New York.
Just months after the election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, candidates backed by the DSA and allied progressive organizations swept Democratic primary elections that many political observers viewed as a referendum on the party’s ideological direction.
Among the most notable victories were Brad Lander’s defeat of incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman in New York’s 10th Congressional District, Claire Valdez’s victory over Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso in the 7th District, and Darializa Avila Chevalier’s upset of five-term incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat in New York’s 13th Congressional District.
Overall, nine of the 10 New York City candidates backed by the DSA won their Democratic primaries, further cementing the organization’s growing influence in the nation’s largest city and demonstrating that democratic socialist candidates can compete beyond isolated local races.
Outside New York, the trend continued.
In Colorado, Melat Kiros defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in one of the cycle’s biggest primary upsets. Kiros campaigned without accepting corporate PAC contributions and criticized DeGette’s fundraising practices and foreign policy positions, presenting herself as an alternative to the Democratic establishment.
While socialist movements have existed in the United States for more than a century, democratic socialism remained largely on the political margins for decades. That began to change following Sen. Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020, which introduced millions of Americans to democratic socialist ideas and energized a younger generation of progressive activists.
Although Sanders never won the Democratic nomination, his campaigns helped reshape the party’s left flank by elevating issues such as universal healthcare, tuition-free public college, stronger labor protections, and economic inequality into the mainstream Democratic conversation.
Today, the movement’s most recognizable elected officials include Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and several members of the congressional “Squad,” who have helped normalize the democratic socialist label among younger Democratic voters and increasingly challenged party leadership from the left.
For LGBTQ voters, democratic socialist candidates have frequently positioned themselves among the Democratic Party’s strongest advocates for transgender rights, particularly as the Trump administration has sought to restrict access to gender-affirming healthcare, military service, and other legal protections for transgender Americans.
The next major test for the movement may come in the Midwest.
In Michigan, progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a closely watched Democratic Senate primary, while in Wisconsin, DSA-backed Francesca Hong is seeking her party’s nomination for governor. The outcomes of those races could offer another measure of whether democratic socialism’s recent gains represent a lasting realignment within the Democratic Party or are concentrated primarily in deep-blue urban districts.
