LGBTQ political candidates see surge in threats, harassment: report
Majority fear physical attack, discouraging them from running
A new study reveals that LGBTQ candidates running for public office are seeing an unprecedented amount of harassment and threats as President Trump and his far-right MAGA supporters continue to strip protections for minority groups at all levels of government.
The LGBTQ+ Victory Institute, the nation’s largest LGBTQ candidate training and leadership organization, recently partnered with Loyola Marymount University to collect data on the rising political violence experienced by LGBTQ candidates. The organization is closely affiliated with the LGBTQ+ Victory Fund, its sister political action arm dedicated to helping LGBTQ candidates get elected.
The Washington Blade sat down with Evan Low, president and CEO of the LGBTQ+ Victory Institute and LGBTQ+ Victory Fund, to discuss what the data reveals about the climate LGBTQ candidates have found themselves in.
Low argued that the findings cannot be separated from the broader political environment facing LGBTQ Americans in 2026. Anti-transgender legislation continues to surge across the country while federal recognition of LGBTQ communities has diminished. This is the second consecutive year Trump has declined to recognize June as Pride month. He also made no public statement commemorating Juneteenth, the anniversary marking the emancipation of enslaved people in the United States.
The survey included 215 LGBTQ+ candidates who ran for office between 2023 and 2025 from 42 states, Puerto Rico, and Washington, D.C., and asked about their experiences while running for office.
The data, while not particularly surprising given the highly divisive political era we have been living through under Trump 2.0, contains stark findings showing that LGBTQ candidates are not only finding it more difficult to run for office — something protected under the First and Fourteenth Amendments — but that it has also become increasingly dangerous for openly LGBTQ candidates to do so.
One of the report’s most significant findings focuses on what happens before an LGBTQ person’s name ever appears on a ballot or yard sign: widespread fear among prospective candidates. Nearly 9 in 10 candidates worried that running as an openly LGBTQ+ person would increase their risk of harassment or attack, while 4 in 5 feared physical violence.
Key Takeaways From the Data
Harassment Is the Norm — Not the Exception: Nearly two-thirds of LGBTQ candidates experienced in-person harassment, while nearly 8 in 10 faced online abuse, with many encountering it regularly.
The escalation from rhetoric to serious threats mirrors the current political climate. One in three candidates received death threats online, and one in seven experienced them in person, highlighting the severity of the current threat environment.
Campaigns Altered by Safety Concerns: More than half of candidates changed how or where they campaigned due to safety fears, and nearly 1 in 5 described the impact as significant — limiting public engagement and visibility.
Security Out of Reach: Fewer than 1 in 10 candidates could afford private security, even as threats escalated, underscoring a growing inequity in who can safely run for office.
Severe Mental Health Impact: Nearly two-thirds of candidates said attacks negatively impacted their mental health, with some reporting long-term trauma and lasting psychological effects.
“What we’re seeing is not just harassment, it’s a systemic challenge to participation,” said Elliot Imse, the now former executive director of LGBTQ+ Victory Institute. “When candidates are forced to change their behavior, limit public engagement, or reconsider running altogether because of safety concerns, that’s not just a personal issue — it’s a breakdown in the conditions required for a healthy democracy.”
“This isn’t theoretical — I, like so many LGBTQ+ candidates and elected leaders, have lived it,” said Daniel Hernandez, vice president of political programs at LGBTQ+ Victory Fund. “From surviving gun violence to having my own campaign office targeted, I know how real these threats are and how deeply they affect candidates, their teams, and their families. The LGBTQ+ Victory Institute has been doing this work for years — preparing candidates, supporting them through these challenges, and making sure they’re not facing it alone. This report makes clear the stakes are higher than ever. If we want people to step up and serve, we have to meet this moment with the resources, support, and commitment to their safety demands.”
Low, who before leading the Victory organizations was an openly gay elected official representing California’s 26th Assembly District, which includes portions of Silicon Valley and San Jose, views the findings as both a political violence issue and a threat to democracy itself.
“We’re living in a moment in a time in which the pendulum is swinging backwards,” Low told the Blade. “We’ve seen a historic amount of anti-LGBTQ+ legislative proposals across this country. So naturally, when members of our community are targeted, it gives that license then to be harassed and discriminated against accordingly. It absolutely is a challenge to democracy.”
The data also shows that LGBTQ candidates face unique barriers to entry — many of them financial. Low argued that reducing those barriers would help diversify candidate pools and create a more representative democracy.
“Does [the current system] disproportionately then impact and limit the segment within our populations to serve? The answer is absolutely yes. When you think about the increased challenges of a barrier to entry– that’s why we’re focused on doing the report in the first place. It also then goes to show the importance of how we utilize taxpayer dollars and budgets accordingly to help encourage and support members of the community to run for office.”
He used that point to emphasize the importance of the LGBTQ+ Victory Institute, not only in collecting data on these trends but also in helping LGBTQ candidates navigate them.
“That’s the fundamental reason why there’s the need for the Victory Fund of the Victory Institute,” he said. “It’s to say that the members of our community will not face this or run alone. They should know that there is a national network, a national organization that will be the wind in their sails to help guide them.”
So far in 2026, the Victory Fund has endorsed at least 249 candidates.
In addition to providing financial support, the Victory Institute helps LGBTQ candidates prepare for the realities of the campaign trail, including coping with harassment, threats, and personal security concerns.
Low expanded on what that reality looks like in 2026 as anti-transgender legislation continues to surge and federal recognition of LGBTQ communities has diminished.
“Part of that discussion is we don’t try to sugarcoat it,” he said when emphasizing the realities facing LGBTQ candidates. “We will speak truth about ‘Here’s how to put a campaign budget together’ and ‘Here’s best practices on public speaking.’ But also we have to deal with showing the unfortunate reality on ‘Here’s how to keep your family safe.’ ‘Here’s how to retain and keep in mind your mental health’…especially when you see members of our community being doxxed constantly by bots and such hate speech.”
He also highlighted the unique challenges facing transgender candidates running for office, particularly as hundreds of bills across the country continue to target transgender people.
“We hear that many times there may be individuals from the community, specifically the trans community, who may want to run for office, but their existence is criminalized, which is to say that they may live in a state or jurisdiction in which it’s criminal to exist; laws prohibiting them from being who they are,” Low said.
“When many of our candidates run for office, they are not running because they are trans, they’re not running because they’re gay or a member of their community, they’re running to advance the quality of life on the key issues on housing affordability, health care, education, you name it, and so these are the campaign issues, but the challenge exists as well.”
Those pressures often lead candidates to question whether running for office is worth the personal toll.
“Many times the candidate and/or elected official will speak candidly with members of our organization to say, ‘Is it worth it anymore? What should I do? Is this something that I should continue? This is taking a personal toll on my family, but I care about the call to service and making a difference in my community.'”
Low also spoke about what he sees as more than simple anti-LGBTQ bias in politics, pointing instead to the growing number of laws targeting LGBTQ people.
“I don’t think it’s simply bias — it’s fact. Again, we can cite laws on the books and proposals across the country, so no wonder why the conversation is so toxic and hostile to members of our community.”
Despite those threats, Low said LGBTQ candidates continue to run for office in record numbers.
“While this political violence report does reflect the hard truth about the challenges to our community, we have seen more candidates apply for an endorsement and sign up for our programs than we’ve ever seen before. We have seen more candidates run for federal office than we ever have had in the history of our 35 years as an organization. What does that tell us? It tells us that yes, it is a challenging and harmful time, yet members of our community are willing to run toward the front lines and answer the call for service.”
The data shows that queer women and transgender candidates are among those most heavily impacted by political violence and heightened political polarization.
“We’ve seen specifically LGBTQ+ women and members of our trans community being disproportionately impacted by [political violence]. When you disaggregate the data, it is also really important to address within our community. We do know anecdotally, as well as from the report, that it may be more challenging for LGBTQ+ women and our trans individuals given some of the other cited conclusions.”
Two of the issues that disproportionately affect transgender candidates and LGBTQ women are mental health challenges and increased security needs.
“What we’ve seen is some of the top demands for services. In many jurisdictions, governmental entities do not have budgets for it– either access to mental health services, as well as public safety services,” he explained. “Security — whether it be surveillance cameras around their homes — those are the key areas. Oftentimes candidates are left to their own devices and may not have access to those key areas to support them.”
Low noted that when LGBTQ candidates are elected, they can advance policies aimed at reducing discrimination, pointing to legislation he championed while serving in California.
“I passed a bill to require Peace Officers Standards and Training curriculum on diversity training for members of the LGBT community. Police officers would have to go through diversity and sensitivity training with respect to members of the LGBT community. That’s something that I very much would like to see amplified, not just state by state, but at the federal level — federal funding to support standards and trainings in dealing with members of the LGBT community.”
“The key data points reflect an increase in not only violence but also intimidation and increased barriers to entry over the years. You can make the direct nexus between that of the increase in anti-LGBTQ legislation and the current rhetoric that exists in this political environment. It’s not just here in the United States — you see it globally as well. So it is something that most certainly we’re seeing increase.”
When asked about the long-term consequences, Low warned that political violence could make American democracy less representative and discourage future generations of LGBTQ leaders from seeking office.
“I think we will likely see a decrease in the diversification of candidates and their lived experiences. It can be insurmountable for those from a younger generation who have to put food on the table and support their families. When it takes political violence to a different level and doxxing and being harassed online, it’s taken on a whole new meaning. We may see that deterioration of the quality and caliber of candidates, or not as much participation from the wide segment of our LGBTQ+ community.”
The Blade also asked how he feels about the future given the current political climate.
“One can always be optimistic and hopeful for the future, but I won’t hold my breath.”
When asked what success would look like for the LGBTQ+ Victory Fund and LGBTQ+ Victory Institute, Low said he hopes to see a decrease in threats against candidates, more LGBTQ people elected to office, and fewer legislative efforts targeting the community.
“I think certainly a decrease when we do this report again and have seen a decrease [in threats] is oftentimes telling. But similarly, seeing less of the legislative proposals in various state houses that are hostile, that criminalize our existence, is another key factor. Those are the two data points that we would cite and highlight as it relates to the political climate with respect to LGBTQ+ leaders.”

sources.text:
Pappas, Sununu win New Hampshire primaries for open US Senate seat
Chris Pappas and John E Sununu won their party nominations for New Hampshire's open Senate seat. Their contest now becomes a crucial test in the battle for Senate control.
US Representative Chris Pappas won the Democratic nomination on Tuesday in the race to succeed US Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, while former US Senator John E Sununu secured the Republican nomination for the open seat. Shaheen, a three-term Democrat, is not seeking re-election.
The results set up a general election between Pappas, who entered the Democratic contest as the frontrunner, and Sununu, who won a crowded Republican primary. Republicans see the seat as a key opportunity as they try to retain control of the Senate.
Pappas is giving up his House seat after four terms. He raised far more money than the other four Democratic candidates and was endorsed by former vice president Kamala Harris. But as the election approached, he faced stronger competition from Karishma Manzur, a research scientist and democratic socialist, who argued that he was too "beholden to special interests".
Pappas currently represents New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District, which covers the eastern half of the state and includes its largest city. He previously served on the governor's Executive Council, a five-member panel that approves state contracts and judicial nominees.
On the Republican side, Sununu defeated former senator Scott Brown and six other candidates to move into the general election. He is seeking to return to the Senate and replace Shaheen, the Democrat who defeated him in 2008. Sununu had earlier served three terms in the House.
Sununu was endorsed by President Donald Trump despite having called him "a loser" during the 2024 presidential campaign. He also had the backing of the Republican establishment in the state.
Brown, who earlier represented Massachusetts and unsuccessfully challenged Shaheen in 2014, accused Sununu of coasting on his name. Sununu's father and younger brother are former governors.
Voters in New Hampshire were also choosing candidates on Tuesday for Congress, governor and the state's 424-seat Legislature. The primary results have now set the stage for a contest between Pappas and Sununu for the Senate seat being vacated by Shaheen.

sources.news_title: John E. Sununu, Chris Pappas projected to win N.H. primary for US Senate - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
MANCHESTER, N.H. — Chris Pappas and John E. Sununu will face off in the Nov. 3 general election to represent the Granite State in the US Senate, according to the Associated Press.
Pappas, 46, is projected to win the Democratic nomination on Tuesday, defeating progressive rival Karishma Manzur, while Sununu, 61, is projected to defeat Scott Brown in the showdown for the Republican nomination.
Pappas, the current US representative for New Hampshire’s First Congressional District, entered the race in April, three weeks after Senator Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement, then secured her prompt endorsement. He maintained a lead in the polls, even as Manzur gained ground.
His victory in the primary represents a win for the moderate wing of the Democratic Party, at a time when more progressive candidates have prevailed in other states.
Pappas, a lifelong Manchester resident whose family has operated the Puritan Backroom Restaurant for decades, would be the first openly gay man to serve in the US Senate. He has been married to lawyer Vann Bentley since 2023.
Sununu is hoping to win back the seat he lost to Shaheen in 2008. His success or failure in the general election could prove pivotal in deciding which party holds the Senate majority for the second half of President Trump’s term.
Trump endorsed Sununu despite their past differences. In the 2024 campaign cycle, Sununu had backed Nikki Haley for the GOP presidential nomination and called Trump a “loser.” Still, the president lent his support in February, solidifying Sununu’s status as the front-runner for the Republican nomination.
Brown, 66, who represented Massachusetts in the US Senate from 2010 to 2013 and later served as a Trump-appointed ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa, had been the first Republican candidate to enter New Hampshire’s Senate race. But his polling and fund-raising numbers trailed Sununu, whose family name represents a political dynasty in the state.
New Hampshire’s past governors include Sununu’s younger brother Chris Sununu and their father, John H. Sununu, who served as White House chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush.

Sununu set to take on Pappas for US Senate in New Hampshire
U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas and former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu will face off for U.S. Senate in November in New Hampshire.
The Democratic and Republican primary races were called by The Associated Press almost immediately after polls closed Tuesday.
Sununu had been leading in the primary polls for much of the race. He thanked his supporters before outlining some of the priorities he would be talking about on the campaign trail.
"We also need to shake up Washington with real reform," Sununu said. What does that mean? Let's start with term limits. No more career politicians. Second, let's make members of Congress pay full price for their health care. No more free rides until they fix what they broke. And third, if like Chris Pappas you vote to shut down government, you don't get paid."
Sununu spent part of his speech attacking Pappas.
"Chris Pappas is a career politician," he said. "He has served in office pretty much every day of his adult life. He's not an independent voice for New Hampshire."
The Associated Press also quickly called the Democratic race for Pappas, who defeated Karishma Manzur.
Speaking to his supporters, Pappas called back to the birth of the country, noting that New Hampshire wrote the first state constitution.
"These folks inked independence into the fabric of what it means to be a Granite Stater, and they laid the foundation for New Hampshire and the United States of America to come into being in the first place," Pappas said. "All these years later, we cherish the fundamental principles of democracy, even as they're being tested as never before."
Pappas alluded to President Donald Trump in his speech. Keeping New Hampshire's Senate seat in Democratic hands is seen as a national priority for the party as it looks to wrest control of the Senate from Republicans.
"We don't believe in kings in New Hampshire, because in America, it's of, by and for the people," Pappas said. "And we the people get to decide what comes next."
Polls have shown the race between Sununu and Pappas to be tight, and Pappas called on his supporters to help to victory in November.
"Let's win this race," he said. "Let's put our state and our country on a better path to the future. Let's save American democracy. Let's stand up to a reckless, out-of-touch president and his hand-picked candidate John Sununu, and let's win this for New Hampshire."
Manzur told her supporters that the Democratic Party needs to unite to defeat Trump and Sununu, and she said the best way to do that is to support Pappas.
But in an interview with News 9, Manzur stopped short of explicitly saying she would endorse Pappas. She said she wants to have a conversation with the Democratic nominee.
"I'm going to keep it between me and Chris until we're ready to tell others," she said. "This was not about a party. This was, of course, to protect democracy and to save people."
Call interrupts Brown's speech
Brown thanked his supporters as the race was called.
"It's been a really, really fun journey," he said. "I have thoroughly enjoyed this race probably more than anyone."
Brown was interrupted at the podium as Sununu called him.
"So that's how you do it New Hampshire," Brown said. "You do it the New Hampshire way. When it's over, you join forces."

U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas swiftly defeated progressive opponent Karishma Manzur in a Democratic Senate primary in New Hampshire on Tuesday, capping off one of several races in which criticism of Israel and AIPAC became prominent talking points.
The Associated Press called the race just an hour after polls closed, at 6 p.m., when 22% of the votes had been counted. As the night wore on, with 88% of the votes tallied, Pappas had accrued 65% of the votes to Manzur’s 32.8%.
Israel featured heavily in the race, with both Pappas and Manzur attacking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Pappas, however, supports Israel’s right to security and condemned the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack on Israel, whereas Manzur questioned Israel’s right to respond to it.
“Today, the voters of New Hampshire have sent a clear message: They’re fed up with what’s happening in our politics, and they’re ready for change,” Pappas told supporters on Tuesday evening. “We’ve got to turn the page on Donald Trump’s reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy.”
Having secured the Democratic nomination, Pappas is seeking to fill the seat of three-term Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is not seeking reelection this year. As he and Manzur spoke to the press during the final weeks of the campaign, their messaging often included condemnations of Israeli leadership.
New Hampshire Democrats chose Pappas, a four-term congressman, as their Senate nominee at a time when their party is hoping to take control of both houses of Congress. Their selection of Pappas, seen as the establishment candidate, could play a pivotal role in November, in a swing state where many voters still split tickets.
Pappas will face former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement, in the general election. Sununu served one term in the Senate, from 2003 to 2009, immediately following three terms in the U.S. House.
Two other Democratic primaries, for neighboring U.S. House seats, likewise focused outsized attention on Israel in recent weeks. But one of the races featured a decisive victory on Tuesday, while in the other there was a very narrow margin between the two candidates.
Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a one-term incumbent, trounced progressive state lawmaker Paige Beauchemin in the 2nd Congressional District, which includes New Hampshire’s capital, Concord, and the city of Nashua. The AP declared Goodlander the projected winner an hour after polls closed. Later in the night, with 84% of the votes tallied, Goodlander had 81.5% to Beauchemin’s 18.3%.
In the next-door Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District, City Councilor Stefany Shaheen narrowly defeated former U.S. Marine Capt. Maura Sullivan in a contest that included numerous other candidates. According to the Associated Press, Shaheen had 37.3% of the votes compared to Sullivan’s 35%, with 91% of the ballots tallied.
The winner of that race will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo, an automotive executive who has Trump’s support, in the November election.
Shaheen is a healthcare advocate and daughter of Jeanne Shaheen, whose Senate seat Pappas is hoping to secure in November. Her opponent, Sullivan, served as the assistant secretary for Veteran Affairs in the Obama administration.
Similar to the U.S. Senate primary hopefuls, candidates in these two races seemed to share near-unanimous disdain for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. They, too, had a spectrum of opinions on the Jewish state, with moderates asserting Israel’s right to defend itself and progressive placing most of the blame for the Gaza war on Israel.
The candidates in the U.S. House races also spent significant airtime in recent weeks blasting the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group. AIPAC has rejected comparisons to corporate PACs, noting that it is membership driven, and claims to be transparent about its funds.
Both Shaheen and Beauchemin accused their opponents of taking AIPAC funds, simply because donors who contributed to the lobby also gave to their campaigns. Sullivan and Goodlander denied these allegations, maintaining that they took no money from AIPAC.

sources.news_title: Sununu, Pappas cruise to NH Senate primary wins, setting up marquee fall race
sources.text:
New Hampshire primary voters have served up what should be the closest U.S. Senate election here in a decade by nominating former Sen. John E. Sununu, a Rye Republican, to face off against four-term, Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas of Manchester.
The showdown should rival the epic battle of 2016 when two-term Democratic Gov. Maggie Hassan of Newfields barely unseated one-term, GOP Sen. Kelly Ayotte of Nashua.
That’s because it features one member of the most storied, GOP political families in recent history against the Democratic Party’s fastest rising star in years.
The nation’s political leadership from President Donald Trump to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer will be watching this one closely over the next eight weeks.
The Democratic hopes of taking back the Senate on Nov. 3 must start with Pappas taking the place of retiring, three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, 79.
For the GOP, New Hampshire has become a welcome escape valve, a seat that it could flip in a year in which Republicans are having to play defense to try and hold onto seats in the red states of Texas, Ohio and Alaska.
Shortly after all polls closed at 8 p.m. Associated Press called the races for Sununu and Pappas.
With 17% of the vote reported, Sununu led former, Massachusetts Republican Sen. Scott Brown, 70% to 25% with the rest cast for little-known hopefuls also on the ballot.
Pappas led Exeter scientist Karishma Manzur, a first-time candidate for elective office, by a smaller margin with 62% to 36% with 27% of the vote counted.
The gloves are off already
Sununu and Pappas started their battle weeks ago with their own campaigns and allies spending millions of dollars on dueling attack ads.
Pappas, 46, went direct to camera, accusing Sununu, 61, of losing his Senate seat in 2008 only to cash in and make up to $35 million in consulting fees for Big Oil, Big Pharma and Big Tech.
Sununu responded by accusing Pappas of opposing some of the biggest federal tax cuts in American history while serving as a toady of the House Democratic establishment, especially under former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
They agree on one thing — the winner of this race will be the one that the greatest number of voters believe will do more to lower costs for working families.
“It’s been a great night. We have had a great result. This is a big win, an exciting win,” Sununu said in victory remarks at McIntyre Ski Area in Manchester with his wife, Kitty
A short time later and a small distance away at the Pappas family-owned, Puritan Conference & Event Center, Pappas returned fire first at President Trump.
“He says we are living in a golden age. I think he’s living on a different planet because does this feels like a Golden Age to you?” Pappas asked rhetorically.
Pappas accused Sununu of using his one term in the Senate to cash in on millions he earned in consulting fees.
“It is not the time to turn to a failed politician of the past,” Pappas said, vowing to work to close the revolving door between “Congress and K Street (lobbyist row).”
Early on, Brown conceded to and then endorsed Sununu.
“I want to thank everybody for all their support. It has been a fun journey,” said Brown at his Manchester campaign offices. “This is how you do it in New Hampshire. You fight hard and if you come up short, you close ranks.”
Republican National Chairman Joe Gruters said winning New Hampshire's seat is a top priority and the Senate Leadership Fund kicked off a $17 million ad buy attacking Pappas relationship with a past lobbyist who he later married.
“Congratulations to John Sununu. Chris Pappas is a weak do-nothing Democrat seeking a promotion he did not earn. Pappas has fallen in line with the radical left, voted with national Democrats at every turn, and abandoned New Hampshire. Sununu is a leader with a proven record who will put New Hampshire first, oppose tax hikes, fight for the rights of Granite Staters and is ready to flip this seat," Gruters said.
Brown could never get a clean shot at Sununu, who won this race by going back to his playbook 24 years earlier.
In her remarks to supporters, Manzur didn’t endorse Pappas but said it’s pivotal to stop the Trump policies and oppose Sununu’s election and that she would be talking with Pappas in the coming days.
Back in 2002, Sununu, then a three-term House member, took on Sen. Bob Smith, R-N.H., who had embarrassed himself and his state by leaving the GOP to wage a quixotic, third-party White House run in 2000.
After it failed miserably, Smith returned to the party and the Senate leadership and got a new committee chairmanship.
At the urging of many GOP leaders, Sununu jumped in and spent that long summer dodging any contact with Smith.
The incumbent Smith, with campaign manager Corey Lewandowski in tow, was reduced to crisscrossing the state for weeks trying to shame Sununu to face him.
Sununu, then 38, did debate Smith, then 61, a few times, but by then the lead was so big it didn’t matter.
Brown couldn’t get Sununu in the ring
This time, Brown was kept at arm’s length from the outset.
Last February, Trump endorsed Sununu, who had never backed Trump’s presidential runs, passing over Brown, 66, who had been ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Trump’s first term.
The Senate Republican majority elite followed suit, which also turned off the spigot of campaign cash for Brown, who badly lagged the frontrunner in fundraising.
Brown said Sununu met him at only one political forum in Hampton in June.
“‘It’s Still The People’s Seat’ is more than a slogan,” Brown’s campaign said on primary day.
“It is a promise that the people of New Hampshire, not Washington insiders, political consultants, or career politicians should decide who represents them in the United States Senate.”

Echoing Democratic primaries across the country this year that have wrestled with the issue of US support for Israel amid the devastation in Gaza, Pappas received criticism from his rival over his voting record in Congress and his relationship with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
But Pappas prevailed in the contentious race with a focus on affordability concerns, a vocal defense of safety-net programs, and a strong electoral track record, while also benefiting from about $4.8 million in outside spending, according to AdImpact data.
His victory could give Democrats a more clear-cut path to holding onto the seat in November than Manzur would have. But Sununu’s strong name recognition and Senate record could prove troublesome for Pappas.
A Republican governor in Harris territory
Ayotte, a former US senator and state attorney general, is one of only two GOP governors seeking reelection this cycle in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.
She campaigned on tougher public safety policies, drawing on her experience as a prosecutor, as well as expanding affordable housing and combating new taxes. She defeated two primary challengers.
In her time as governor, Ayotte has had an occasionally antagonistic relationship with New Hampshire’s legislature, despite the body being controlled by her own party. In the last legislative session, Ayotte vetoed 33 bills. Lawmakers overturned seven of the vetoes, clashing with the governor over issues like criminal justice and education.
With Warmington running unopposed in her primary, Republicans turned their attention to the former New Hampshire executive councilor’s campaign early and sought to tie her to the opioid crisis.
The Democrat previously worked for Purdue Pharma, which produced the highly addictive painkiller OxyContin, and in the early 2000s she fought against a state bill meant to make it more difficult to get a prescription for the drug. She has since said she was not aware of how dangerous the drug was at the time.
While Harris won the state in 2024, Republicans have held a trifecta in the state government for several years.
One Shaheen exits, another enters
When Sen. Jeanne Shaheen leaves the Senate early next year, her daughter could be headed to the House of Representatives at the same time.
Bolstered by support from local labor unions and New Hampshire’s other senator, Democrat Maggie Hassan, Stefany Shaheen defeated a crowded field of primary rivals to secure the Democratic nomination.
In November, she’ll face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo for the Manchester-based swing seat, which Pappas has represented since 2019.
But while she’s likely benefited from name recognition in her bid for New Hampshire’s 1st District, Stefany Shaheen has not been afraid to separate herself from the longtime senator and former New Hampshire governor.
A healthcare advocate and entrepreneur, the younger Shaheen focused her campaign on the issue and publicly broke with her mother when the senator last year voted in support of a deal to end the government shutdown without the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies.
“Improving health care has been the cause of my life. It’s why I am running for Congress. So I cannot support this deal when Speaker Johnson refuses to even allow a vote to extend health care tax credits,” she said in a statement at the time.
DiLorenzo is a first-time candidate endorsed by Trump. He leaned heavily on his experience in the private sector as a real estate developer and auto dealer during the GOP primary, funneling more than $1.7 million of his own money into his campaign.
The longtime GOP donor was also bolstered by support from key members of Republican House leadership as they look to flip the 1st District and expand their razor-thin majority in the chamber.

Pappas and Sununu set up marquee Senate clash in New Hampshire
Stefany Shaheen wins Democratic nomination for battleground 1st District
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu won their respective Senate primaries Tuesday in New Hampshire, formalizing a fall matchup for an open seat that both sides have already begun fighting over.
With over 80 percent of votes counted, Pappas was leading biochemist Karishma Manzur, 65 percent to 33 percent, The Associated Press reported, while Sununu was ahead of former Massachusetts Sen. Scott P. Brown, 68 percent to about 27 percent, with close to 80 percent of the estimated vote in.
In the race for the battleground House seat Pappas is vacating, former Portsmouth City Councilor Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, clinched the Democratic nomination, besting a crowded primary field. With nearly 90 percent of votes counted, she was leading Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan 37 percent to 35 percent just before 1 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, the AP reported.
The Senate race to succeed the senior Shaheen in New Hampshire could be crucial to deciding control of the chamber this fall, and both parties are bracing for a tight general election. Pappas has warned Democrats not to take the contest for granted, even though Republicans haven’t won a Senate race in the state since 2010.
Republicans, though, have been upbeat over recent polling that showed a margin-of-error race between Sununu and Pappas. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales changed its race rating last week from Tilt Democratic to Toss-up.
“As Senator, I’ll have just one job: stand up for the people of New Hampshire every single day,” Sununu said in a statement Tuesday. “We will keep listening, keep working, and stay laser-focused on the economy, jobs, and making life more affordable.”
Senate Democrats have expanded the battleground map this year and are competing for seats in red states such as Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. They need a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber, but a Republican victory in New Hampshire could be an important step in helping the party defend its Senate majority.
Both parties are expeted to cast their nominee as best suited to represent the politically savvy state, and, perhaps even more so, to portray the opposing candidate as a Washington insider.
“After personally recruiting Sununu to run, Leader John Thune and Senate Republicans have expanded the map and are poised to flip the Granite State,” Alex Latcham, the executive director of the GOP super PAC Senate Leadership Fund, said in a statement. “From now until November, SLF will spend every day highlighting John E. Sununu’s positive vision for New Hampshire while exposing the corruption, self-dealing, and radical record of Washington insider Chris Pappas.”
Sununu, who has President Donald Trump’s endorsement, is attempting a political comeback 18 years after he lost reelection to Jeanne Shaheen after a term in the Senate. He entered the Senate race last year with significant name recognition, given his family’s long involvement in New Hampshire politics. His father is a former governor and served as chief of staff to President George H. W. Bush. His brother Chris Sununu served four terms as governor before retiring in 2024, and Republicans first tried to recruit him for the open Senate race.
Pappas’ primary victory Tuesday came after a recent poll showed a tightening race against Manzur, who had run as an outsider and challenged the congressman from the left.
Pappas, who held a massive fundraising edge over Manzur heading into election day, had already begun training his sights on the general election. He accused Sununu of seeking to enrich himself by working as a lobbyist after leaving the Senate.
If elected in November, Pappas would be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate. Democrats argue that the four-term House member, whose family owns the Puritan Backroom, a Manchester restaurant credited with inventing the chicken tender, is a good fit for the state. Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer and New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, sought to draw a contrast Tuesday night between Pappas and Sununu.
“Chris Pappas is a small business owner and descendant of Greek immigrants who is grounded in the values, people, and places of New Hampshire,” they said. “John Sununu went to Washington almost thirty years ago and voted to serve the interests of Wall Street, Big Oil, and Big Pharma in the Senate, then sold out to make millions off those same industries.”
House races
In 1st District, which takes up parts of eastern New Hampshire, Stefany Shaheen prevailed over a crowded Democratic field, which included a handful of candidates who dropped out before the primary.
The race between Shaheen and Sullivan had grown increasingly sour in the final weeks of the campaign, with both sides slinging attacks over fundraising and Shaheen’s well-known name also lingered over the race – her mother also previously served as governor, while her father, Billy Shaheen, has long been involved in state Democratic politics.
Sullivan, who worked at the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Pentagon during the Obama administration, was making her second bid for the seat after a runner-up finish to Pappas in the 2018 primary.
Shaheen will next face Republican businessman Anthony DiLorenzo, who was leading his nearest opponent, businesswoman Hollie Noveletsky, 51 percent to 26 percent, with about 85 percent of the vote counted, according to the AP.
DiLorenzo, the owner of several car dealerships, had the endorsement of Trump and the National Republican Congressional Committee. He largely self-funded his campaign, loaning himself $1.8 million through Aug. 19.
New Hampshire’s 1st District regularly flipped between the parties until Pappas first won the seat in 2018. But without an incumbent on the ballot, Republicans are hopeful that the district will return to its previously competitive status.
Inside Elections rates the race Lean Democratic.
Meanwhile, the state’s 2nd District, freshman Rep. Maggie Goodlander easily clinched the Democratic nomination over state Rep. Paige Beauchemin. She will face a rematch of her 2024 race against activist Lily Tang Williams, who won the Republican nomination in what is her third straight bid for the seat.
Inside Elections rates the race Likely Democratic.

The News
New Hampshire’s premier Senate race is on after party leaders secured their top choices in what’s shaping up to be one of the tightest contests in the entire country come November.
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will face former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu after Pappas easily defeated progressive Karishma Manzur in the Democratic primary. And Sununu crushed former GOP Sen. Scott Brown, a show of dominance attributable to President Donald Trump’s endorsement, backing from many GOP senators and his family’s dynastic reputation in New Hampshire.
Now, the general election looms and polls show the race is a little too close for comfort for Democrats in a state where they haven’t lost a Senate race since 2010.
“I do think Chris Pappas is in a tighter race than most of the political class recognize,” Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., told Semafor before Tuesday night’s primary results. “We have to retain that one.”
Know More
Republicans argue the race could be a game-changer for them because it could blunt Democrats’ momentum in regaining control of the Senate. If Democrats lose New Hampshire’s Senate seat, they have to win five more seats elsewhere in addition to defending their existing territory — a task that’s all but impossible without a titanic wave election.
“After personally recruiting Sununu to run, [Senate Majority] Leader John Thune and Senate Republicans have expanded the map and are poised to flip the Granite State,” said Alex Latcham, who runs the Thune-aligned Senate Leadership Fund super PAC.
To be sure, Pappas has been preparing for a very tight race in a battleground state that has been a consistent bright spot for Democrats in the Trump era. He told Semafor this summer that New Hampshire is “very much a purple state. I think Democrats have done the work to win what ordinarily would be incredibly tough races at the federal level, but that doesn’t change the dynamics of New Hampshire.”

This is a developing story and will be updated as fresh results become available.
New Hampshire voters have selected Democratic Congressman Chis Pappas and former Republican U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu to face off in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. It’s a contest leaders in both parties see as essential to deciding control of the U.S. Senate.
As of 8:20 p.m. Tuesday, Pappas had 62% of the vote, against Karishma Manzur, with 27% of votes tallied. Sununu had 70% against 25% for Scott Brown, with 16% of votes tallied. (See the latest results.)
The race is now down to two candidates whose histories in state politics stretch back decades.
Pappas has represented New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District for four terms. He also served as state representative, country treasurer for Hillsborough County, and executive councilor. He and his family own the Puritan Backroom, a restaurant that has been an institution in Manchester for decades. Few Democrats in New Hampshire are as well-known and well-liked by the party’s mainstream, and from the moment Pappas declared his candidacy more than a year ago, his nomination was seen by Democratic leaders, here and in D.C., as inevitable.
But despite the final margin, Pappas’ win over Manzur, a scientist and progressive activist from Exeter, was tougher than expected, even with Pappas enjoying a massive advantage in both name recognition and campaign cash.
Manzur, a political newcomer, promised to push for Medicare for All, a $25 federal minimum wage, and higher taxes on the wealthy. Throughout her campaign, Manzur also focused on ending U.S. support for Israel, which she says has committed genocide in Gaza. Manzur also repeatedly hammered Pappas for his longstanding ties to the American Israel Political Action Committee, or AIPAC, which has funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars to his campaigns over the years.
Manzur said party leaders in New Hampshire worked to thwart her bid to challenge Pappas, but dogged campaigning – she claims to have put 28,000 miles on a campaign van she often drove herself – as well as support from Democrats disillusioned by their party’s mainstream, lifted Manzur’s bid, making the race far more competitive than early expectations.
Pappas’ campaign worked to cast him as a candidate bent on reform in Washington, but also one who was pragmatic and experienced, in the mold of other successful Democrats like Shaheen and Sen. Maggie Hassan.
Pappas also got a boost from national Democrats: He finished off his primary campaign by courting voters over the weekend with Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, who joined Pappas separately on multiple stops during his campaign’s home stretch.
Sununu, who served in Congress from 1997 to 2003 and in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, is seen by most in his party as the strongest available Republican nominee. His primary race against Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the U.S. Senate from 2010 to 2012 before relocating here to run unsuccessfully for this same seat in 2014, was low-key.
Both former senators repeatedly told voters that they would be “independent” if sent back to Washington, but from the start, the campaign felt like a mismatch.
One reason Sununu had an early clear advantage was name recognition. Due to his own political career as well as those of his brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu, and his father, former Gov. John H. Sununu, his surname has been synonymous with GOP politics in New Hampshire for decades.
Another reason for the mismatch was Sununu’s support from President Donald Trump and national Republican leaders.
Sununu had once been a vocal critic of the president, but Trump endorsed Sununu early on, and without Trump’s endorsement, Brown faced little chance of overcoming Sununu’s advantages in name recognition and fundraising.
Sununu himself has largely avoided talking about Trump’s backing. He’s said he disagreed with Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran, and offered muted criticism of Trump's tariff-driven trade policies.
But mostly Sununu has trained his focus on criticizing Pappas, who he says votes almost exclusively with leaders in his party, and favors higher taxes.

Sununu, Pappas win NH Senate primaries setting up key race
Former Republican Sen. John Sununu will battle Democrat Rep. Chris Pappas in a high-stakes U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire as the GOP is seeking to hold its majority by flipping the seat currently held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
Pappas emerged victorious Tuesday, holding off a late-surging challenge from scientist Karishma Manzur to win the Democratic Senate primary, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ projected shortly after the polls closed at 8 p.m.
Sununu, the former New Hampshire GOP senator endorsed by President Donald Trump, handily defeated fellow former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown, also minutes after polls closed.
The Granite State, which former Vice President Kamala Harris carried by less than 3 percentage points in 2024, is one of the few Democratic Senate seats that could be flipped in a year when Republicans are mostly on defense amid Trump's low approval ratings.
Republican officials mostly backed Sununu, whose father and brother are both former New Hampshire governors.
A poll conducted by Emerson College earlier this year showed a hypothetical general election matchup between Sununu and Pappas was a virtual tie. Both parties are expected to invest heavily into New Hampshire.
Further down the state's ballot is a race to fill Pappas' seat on the Democratic side. Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the outgoing senator is leading Maura Sullivan, a retired Marine, with most of the precincts having been counted.
RNC chair praises Sununu's win, bashes Pappas
Terry Collins and Margie Cullen
Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters on Tuesday heaped praise on New Hampshire GOP Senate candidate John Sununu, while also bashing his Democratic challenger, Rep. Chris Pappas, in the process.
"Chris Pappas is a weak do-nothing Democrat seeking a promotion he did not earn," Gruters said in a statement about the congressman. "Pappas has fallen in line with the radical left, voted with national Democrats at every turn, and abandoned New Hampshire."
Gruters' comments come as Republicans attempt to flip the seat, held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, with a Sununu victory over Pappas in November's general election.
Pappas beat scientist and progressive candidate Karishma Manzur to win the Democratic primary, and Sununu, the former New Hampshire GOP senator endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown.
"Sununu is a leader with a proven record who will put New Hampshire first, oppose tax hikes, fight for the rights of Granite Staters and is ready to flip this seat," Gruters added.
Tight primary for Pappas seat
Phillip M. Bailey
Rep. Chris Pappas running for Senate left his House seat vacant, which attracted a crowded seven-person field in the Democratic primary.
With about 62% of precincts reporting, Stefany Shaheen is leading by about two percentage points, or less than 1,000 votes, over Maura Sullivan. Shaheen is the daughter of outgoing Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and was the initial frontrunner, but Sullivan gained ground with attacks on Shaheen for being unfairly advantaged by her mother's stature.
Pappas early favorite to win NH Senate, expert says
Terry Collins
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas has an early edge against former Republican Sen. John Sununu in a must-watch U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire, according to one renowned political expert.
Pappas defeated scientist and progressive candidate Karishma Manzur to win the Democratic Senate primary, and Sununu, the former New Hampshire GOP senator backed by President Donald Trump, beat former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown.
The anticipated race sets up whether Sununu can flip the Senate seat currently held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen to the GOP.
"Pappas is still favored, in my view," said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of the nonpartisan Sabato's Crystal Ball newsletter at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, told USA TODAY late Tuesday. "This is ultimately a Democratic-leaning state in federal races, and this is a Democratic leaning year.
"That is a lot for Sununu to overcome," Kondik concluded.
Scott Brown's second failed comeback
James Powel
Former Sen. Scott Brown was once a rising star in Republican politics, but he just failed to resurrect his political career for the second time with his primary loss to former Sen. John Sununu Tuesday.
Brown went to Washington from Massachusetts following the death of Sen. Ted Kennedy. In 2010, Brown was a state senator who defeated state Attorney General Martha Coakley in a special election upset.
The surprise outcome in the overwhelmingly Democratic state broke Democratic Party's short-lived filibuster-proof 60-vote Senate supermajority.
Brown was defeated in 2012 by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, after which he won the 2014 Republican nomination for Senate in New Hampshire, but he was beaten in the general election by then Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
Brown takes call from Sununu during speech
James Powel
Brown took a call from Sununu during his concession speech, just after saying he "thoroughly enjoyed" the race.
The conversation was brief and afterwards Brown said he would "join forces" with the GOP Senate nomination winner adding that it's the "New Hampshire way."
"He has a long journey ahead of him," Brown said.
Lily Tang Williams wins GOP primary for NH 2nd District
Margie Cullen
Lily Tang Williams, the 2024 Republican nominee, has won the Republican primary for New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ project.
She defeated Dan Nicholson, of Nashua, and Victor Orlando, of Hollis.
The district, which covers the western, northern and some southern parts of New Hampshire, including the cities of Concord and Nashua, is rated “Solid D” by the Cook Political Report.
Rep. Maggie Goodlander wins Democratic primary for New Hampshire's 2nd District
Margie Cullen
Rep. Maggie Goodlander has fended off a primary challenge from state Rep. Paige Beauchemin to win the Democratic primary for New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ project.
Goodlander is seeking her second term in the district, which covers the western, northern and some southern parts of New Hampshire, including the cities of Concord and Nashua, and is rated “Solid D” by the Cook Political Report.
Trump-endorsed candidate wins GOP primary in NH 2nd District
Margie Cullen
Anthony DiLorenzo, a businessman and first-time candidate, has won the Republican primary for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ project.
He defeated businesswoman Hollie Noveletsky, who had been his closest opponent in the polls, as well as Lindsey Anderson and Brian Cole.
DiLorenzo was likely bolstered by President Donald Trump’s endorsement. His win adds to the president’s near-perfect record in GOP primaries this year.
He will advance to the November general election. The race is rated “Likely D” by the Cook Political Report.
Pappas wins Democratic primary for U.S. Senate
Margie Cullen
Rep. Chris Pappas held off a late challenge from the left in scientist Karishma Manzur to win the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ projected shortly after polls closed.
Democrats are aiming to hold this seat, currently held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, to aid in their quest to flip the U.S. Senate, which is narrowly controlled by Republicans. The seat is rated “Lean Democrat” by the Cook Political Report.
Pappas, whose ability to outrun his party allowed him to win four terms in the historically purple 1st District, was considered the more electable candidate in November.
NH Gov. Kelly Ayotte cruises to victory in GOP primary
Margie Cullen
Incumbent Gov. Kelly Ayotte has defeated two little known Republican challengers, Shaun Fife and Bob Wayne McClory, to win the Republican primary for New Hampshire governor, the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ projected shortly after polls closed.
She will face former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington, who was unopposed in the Democratic primary, in her quest for a second term.
Sununu wins GOP Senate primary
Margie Cullen

Trump-backed John Sununu wins Republican nomination for New Hampshire Senate
The president endorsed Sununu, whose brother is former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu, in February, touting him as an "American First patriot" and as the candidate with the strongest backing among conservative leaders in the state.
Former New Hampshire Republican Sen. John Sununu on Tuesday night defeated former Trump ambassador to New Zealand Scott Brown for the Republican nomination to represent New Hampshire in the Senate.
Sununu, who secured President Donald Trump's endorsement earlier this year, defeated Brown with 69.7% of the vote compared to 25.2%, according to the Associated Press.
The president endorsed Sununu, whose brother is former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu, in February, touting him as an "American First patriot" and as the candidate with the strongest backing among conservative leaders in the state.
Sununu will now face Democrat Chris Pappas in November, which comes as Washington Republicans hope to flip the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
