11:38 p.m.: New Hampshire Second Congressional District tees up for rematch
Annabelle Zhang / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Incumbent Maggie Goodlander, N.H.-2, will once again face Republican nominee Lily Tang Williams in the general election race to represent New Hampshire’s second congressional district this year. Goodlander was elected to her first term in 2024 after defeating Tang Williams by 6.5% of the vote.
At time of publication, Goodlander is leading N.H. State Rep. Paige Beauchemin in this year’s race to be the Democratic nominee with 82% of the vote, of the 68% of votes counted. Tang Williams, who faced stonemason Michael Anthoy Callis, entrepreneur Dan Nicholson and construction business owner Victor Orlando this year, leads her opponents with 65.6% of the 56% of votes in.
9:28 p.m.: Hanover results are in
Annabelle Zhang / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
The Hanover vote counts are in.
On the Democratic ballot, Cinde Warmington received all 1,377 votes for governor in an uncontested race. Chris Pappas, D-N.H.-1, defeated Karishma Manzur 1,130 to 405 to become the Democratic nominee for senator to replace three-term senator Jeanne Shaheen. Incumbent Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H.-2, defeated N.H. state senator Paige Beauchemin 1,328 to 197. She will face Republican nominee Lily Tang Williams, who received all 85 votes in Hanover, for a rematch of their 2024 contest in November.
Incumbent Karen Liot Hill ’00 received 1,345 votes in an uncontested race for executive councilor. Suzanne Prentiss received 1,321 votes for state senator.
All four incumbents currently representing Grafton County’s 12th district were re-nominated. Dartmouth lecturer Ellen Rockmore and government professor Russell Muirhead received 1,200 and 1,237 votes, respectively. Terry Spahr and Mary Hakken-Philips received 1,177 and 1,267 votes, respectively.
Incumbent Jillian E. Myers received 1,138 votes to become the Democratic nominee for sheriff. Martha Ann Hornick received 1,234 votes for county attorney. Michael Cryans received 1,337 votes in an uncontested race for county treasurer. Brie Choat received 1,286 votes for register of deeds. Sharon Modjeska received 1,264 votes for register of probate. George Sykes received 1,272 votes for county commissioner. All six candidates were the only names on the Democratic ballot in their respective races.
On the Republican ballot, incumbent Gov. Kelly Ayotte received all 151 votes for governor, while John E. Sununu and Scott Brown split the vote for U.S. senator 125 to 32, respectively. Tobin Menard defeated Kim Strathdee 66 to 56 for executive councilor, while Conrad Schoeffter and Kelley Jean Monahan each received 112 votes for state senator and register of deeds, respectively, in uncontested races.
No Republicans ran for the nomination in the races for Grafton District 12 state representative, sheriff, county attorney, register of probate or county commissioner. Country treasurer candidate Brian Dear received no votes. Neither Thomas W. Toner nor Jim Rubens, both of whom ran for delegates to the state convention Grafton District 12, received any votes.
8:46 p.m.: Initial results from the primary elections come in
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Nearly two hours after polls closed in Hanover, initial results from the state primary races are being called.
John E. Sununu won the Republican nomination for U.S. senator for New Hampshire, according to New Hampshire Public Radio. Sununu defeated opponent Scott Brown with 70% and 25% of the vote at 16% votes tallied, respectively.
Chris Pappas won the Democratic nomination for U.S. senator of New Hampshire, according to NHPR. Pappas defeated Karishma Manzur with 62% of the vote at the vote at 27% of votes tallied.
Incumbent Kelly Ayotte won the Republican nomination for New Hampshire governor, according to NBC News. Ayotte defeated Shaun Fife and Bob McClory, with 90% of the vote at 26% ballots tallied.
Cinde Warmington, who was uncontested in the primary elections, won the Democratic nomination for New Hampshire governor, according to NBC News.
7:15 p.m.: Rockefeller Center hosts primary election watch party
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
The Rockefeller Center is hosting a New Hampshire primary watch party, which began at 6:00 p.m.. The event is being held at Hinman Forum, located inside the Rockefeller Center for Public Policy. There are around 25 people — including students, staff and professors — in attendance.
In an interview with The Dartmouth, Rockefeller Center director and government professor Jason Barabas ’93 said he was “surprised” by how non-establishment candidates — such as Zohran Mamdani, now mayor of New York City, and Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for Senate — have gained political traction in “unique” ways in different states throughout recent election cycles. Constituents have a “willingness to not play it safe” with the candidates they elect, he said.
“I think the electorate is in the mood for change, and you saw that with Trump’s election in 2016, and then more recently in the 2024 election,” Barabas said. “The desire for change can happen on the right, as it did for Trump a few times, but it could also happen on the left, too.”
7:00 p.m.: Polls close
Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Polls have now closed. 1693 ballots were machine counted. Around 20 to 25 more must be handcounted, according to Eggleton.
“It struck me as a pretty slow day at the polls, all things considered,” Eggleton said. Out of the 6,553-person voter roll, only 25.8% cast ballots.
Eggleton predicted that unofficial tallies will be available around 8:30 p.m. Official counts will be available later in the evening and posted at the town hall, located at 41 S Main St., on Wednesday morning.
5:52 p.m.: 1,560 votes counted so far
Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Around an hour before polls close, 1,560 ballots have been counted — around 22% of the electorate, according to Eggleton.
“Normally we would expect 500 to 800 Dartmouth students registering, which would bump it up,” he said.
4:27 p.m.: Rabbi Gray on how his religion affects his voting
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Chabad executive director Rabbi Moshe Leib Gray came through the polls at Hanover High School this afternoon, voting in the Democratic primary. He said that he is a “single-issue voter,” taking US-Israel relations under “strong consideration” when voting.
“Being actively Jewish today definitely influences who I’m voting for,” Gray said. “Israel is obviously very important to me, and the relationship between the United States and Israel, and that allyship is important to me, so that’s certainly one of the things that is very high on my list.”
Gray added that he is concerned about the “woke right” and “woke left,” decrying both for being “anti-education.” He praised Dartmouth Dialogues for helping to move out of political “echo chamber.”
3:58 p.m.: Around 1,300 ballots counted so far
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Around 1,300 ballots have been submitted so far, according to Eggleton. This includes 1,274 ballots accounted for electronically and around 25 absentee ballots, though there is not an exact count for the number of absentee ballots submitted yet, Eggleton said.
“The pace [of voting] today has been very slow,” he added.
3:30 p.m.: Students come out to vote
Iris WeaverBell and Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Oak Hill Croo, one of the First-Year Trips support groups, came to the polls after a week of teaching mountain biking to incoming Dartmouth students. Those who were eligible to vote in N.H. cast their ballots, while others joined for fun, according to croolings Ari Graham-Gurland ’27 and Ellie Zimmerman ’27, both of whom voted.
“We have become closer friends … because we’re working First-Year Trips Croo all together, and I thought it was important that we take some time during the day to go out and vote,” Graham-Gurland said.
Zimmerman said the most important issue for her in this election cycle is immigration and policies for international students.
“All the difficulties that I’ve been seeing a lot of international students have on campus has been really disheartening to see, and you could sense that stress in the ’30s as well,” Zimmerman said. “International students on campus are definitely more stressed than they were when I first came to Dartmouth.”
Mischa Telesford ’27 voted to exercise her “civic duty” and to not “squander that as a Black woman.” She also came to the polls to support her friend, Jesse Fitzelle-Jones who has been at the polls volunteering for Karishma Mansur.
Telesford said she voted for Karishma Manzur and Paige Beauchemin because she did not want to support “establishment Democrats” who make “vague promises” about social issues like abortion. She added that she doesn’t support candidates who accept “AIPAC money.”
“I’m sick and tired of needless wars that my taxpayer dollars are going toward,” Telesford said. “I don’t really agree with war to begin with, let alone wars that we are paying for.”
Telesford added that she is “tired of politicians that are fundamentally out of touch” with their constituents and that she hopes for candidates who have an “intersectional understanding of identity.”
3:02 p.m.: Russell Muirhead on campaigning as a professor
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Government professor and State Rep. Russell Muirhead, D-Hanover, campaigned outside the polls at Hanover High in his reelection race today in his uncontested reelection race today. In an interview with The Dartmouth, he said this midterm election is “really all about Trump” for both Democrats and Republicans.
“Trump is dominating American politics, unlike any figure since Franklin Roosevelt,” Muirhead said. “Even though his name is not on the ballot, and even though I think most Republicans wish that this election weren’t about him, I think so long as he’s alive and in office, our elections are, in way or another, going to be about Trump.”
Muirhead said the “Make America Great Again movement” has created “disruption” around core policy discussions, such as trade, tariffs and immigration. He added that as a state representative, he can protect voters’ “access to the ballot.”
“There’s really been an attack on election administration over the last six years in American politics,” Muirhead said. “That attack focuses on states because it’s states that run elections.”
Muirhead also said that, if reelected, he will focus on providing “services to disabled people” and “children of people who’ve been imprisoned” during the next legislative session.
“There are certain populations who are at risk of being evicted,” Muirhead said. “People who really live on the economic margins, where I think we can do a lot to provide a little more security.”
Muirhead said most state house Republicans did not support Trump until 2024, when the president “delivered them to power.” Despite ideological differences, he has many “friends” that he “admires” in the Republican Party.
“They’re public spirited, they’re honest [and] they have good character,” Muirhead said. “We just disagree about a lot of stuff, and I’d rather be in the majority than in the minority, and so would they.”
2:36 p.m.: N.H. assistant attorney general says proper procedures are being followed at Hanover polls
Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
N.H. assistant attorney general Kevin Scura came to observe Hanover polls to ensure election officials were following N.H. election laws.
“We [members of the N.H. Attorney General’s office] go around to all the polls in the state just to go through and make sure that the proper procedures are being followed, according to the statute — mainly for the purpose of increasing voter confidence,” Scura said.
State election officials have faced increased scrutiny from the second Trump administration. President Donald Trump has accused several states — including N.H. — of voter fraud. The Trump administration has unsuccessfully sued for access to N.H.’s and several other states’ voter rolls. In July, U.S. assistant attorney general Harmeet Dhillon ’89 sent a letter to all state election officials threatening criminal prosecution over noncitizen voting.
Scura said the federal government “has not affected” his poll observations.
2:06 p.m.: Hanover residents reflection on the primary elections
Jared Gonzalez Arce and Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Hanover resident Teresa Piotrowski, an independent who usually votes for Democratic candidates, said she voted for Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander in their respective races. Piotrowski said the most important issue for her voting choices was access to home healthcare, but she was unsure if federal elections would increase affordability. In 2022, Teresa’s husband Ted Piotrowski, a retired sociology and anthropology professor at the University of New Hampshire, fell off his bicycle and suffered a traumatic brain injury, despite wearing his helmet, Teresa said. Medicare very rarely covers home healthcare — which Teresa said costs $35 per hour — so Teresa cares for Ted nonstop.
“It’s impossible for me to get anybody to give me a break,” she said in an interview with Ted at the polls this afternoon. “I don’t want to put him in a home.”
Voters seem to be disenchanted with the Trump administration, turning to Democratic candidates as a rejection of the president. Retired carpenter Tom Carney voted in the Democratic primary, saying that he doesn’t see the Republican Party as “standing for democracy.” Carney said he voted for Karishma Manzur because he believes it’s time to pass government onto the “younger generation.”
“We [the older generation] have had our chance, done some good things, done some bad, but I think the next generation needs to take over,” he said.
Carney said getting rid of the “craziness” in politics was top of his mind when casting his ballot today.
Dartmouth psychological and brain sciences professor emeritus Howard Hughes said he voted for Pappas and Goodlander, adding that he hopes the election is the “beginning of the end” for the Trump administration.
“I think that this county desperately needs to send a message to Washington, D.C. that the current administration has to go,” Hughes said.
1:48 p.m.: Just over 1,000 ballots cast so far
Just over 1,000 ballots have been cast so far, according to Eggleton. Turnout still “seems slow to me,” he said.
10:50 a.m.: Turnout is lower than expected so far
Three hundred ninety-nine ballots have been cast so far, according to town moderator Jeremy Eggleton. Five people have registered today, supervisor of the checklist Alison Gorman said.
Eggleton said in an interview that he expected turnout to be higher given that there are “a couple of competitive races.”
“Typically, at the start of the day, there would be a line of people extending out into the parking lot, waiting to come in, and today, there just weren't any,” he said.
Eggleton said there has been “no issues” with student IDs.
9:48 a.m.: Karen Liot-Hill on campaigning and representing Dartmouth
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Karen Liot-Hill ’00, who is running uncontested in the Democratic primary for Executive Council District 2, said she would be visiting “30 out of 100 polling locations” in her district today, which spans western New Hampshire. At the Hanover High School polls, Liot-Hill told The Dartmouth it was good to “be connected with the people that are working for the same goals I am.”
“Any day that I get to be on the trail talking with voters, and especially a day like today, spending time with my fellow Democrats who are on the ballot with me, this is the kind of thing that recharges me and nurtures my soul,” Liot-Hill said.
Though Liot-Hill is currently the only Democrat on the Executive Council, she said there is “a lot” that the council members agree on. She added that the council votes unanimously “95% of the time.”
Liot-Hill said that she wants to focus on “consumer protection” to address affordability, adding that private equity firms are “buying up” affordable housing, such as mobile home parks, and “driving up the rent.”
“We need to look at consumer protection work to make sure that regular people who have been doing everything right are not getting taken advantage of and exploited by out-of-state private equity firms that aren’t invested in our communities,” she said.
Additionally, cost of living is “on a lot of people’s minds” in New Hampshire, she said, adding that affordability has become such a “crisis” that it “creates an opportunity for people to work across the aisle.”
Liot-Hill added that getting to represent the College as part of her district is “special.”
“There’s no doubt that coming to Hanover and doing my studies here at Dartmouth [is] what led me to stay here in New Hampshire and to devote my life and career to trying to make life better,” she said.
9:47 a.m.: Students and professors at the polls say that student-ID law created ‘additional stress’
Iris WeaverBell and Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
H.B. 323, which went into effect in June, bans the use of school-issued IDs to verify identity to obtain a ballot at the polls.
English professor and State Rep. Ellen Rockmore, D-Hanover, said that students should feel “confident in
exercising their constitutional right to vote here in Hanover.”
Rockmore said that it is “logistically challenging” for students to obtain a form of identification in New Hampshire, adding that Democrats want to “maximize voting opportunities” and will “vote down anything that’s going to make voting harder.
“I know how challenging it would be for a Dartmouth first-year student who doesn’t have a car to get to the [Department of Motor Vehicles] in Claremont and get a driver’s license in New Hampshire ,” Rockmore said. She added that the Claremont DMV is “far away and inconvenient.”
Himstreet — who switched his voter registration from Oregon to Hanover during the 2024 election — said that restricting school I.D. as a valid way of obtaining a ballot adds an “unnecessary additional barrier” that “restricts people’s right to vote.”
“I think the fact that you’re here for the majority of the year and being a part of this community means your vote should matter,” Himstreet said.
Trace Ribble ’29, who voted for Manzur and Beuchemin this morning although is not confident that either will win, said that H.B. 323 is “absolutely” a barrier for students. Ribble said he brought his passport to vote.
Prior to the enactment of the new voter ID law, “it would have been so easy for me to vote because everyone always has their student ID on them,” he said.
Reichman said that although she has a drivers license, the law “added additional stress” because she is “concerned for potential voters … who were unaware that the law had changed.”
Fitzelle-Jones called the law “ridiculous” and “meant to attack Democrats,” but said it did not affect him “that much.”
9:20 a.m.: Dartmouth Democrats leaders support multiple primary candidates
Iris WeaverBell and Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Dartmouth Democrats president Bea Reichman ’27 was at the polls this morning, volunteering for Goodlander in her personal capacity. Dartmouth Democrats does not endorse candidates in primaries to allow for “diverse perspectives” within the chapter, Reichman said in an interview.
Reichman supports Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H.-1, in his senate bid. He faces progressive scientist and political outsider Karishma Manzur in today’s Democratic primary.
“I believe that Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander’s experience in Congress, and their voting record, has proven that they deeply care about the people of New Hampshire,” she said. “They’re extremely present in New Hampshire, and they care very deeply about the mission of our state and our community.”
Specifically, Goodlander’s “foreign policy experience really sets her apart from other candidates” in the race for House seat representing New Hampshire’s second district.
Reichman said reproductive health is “top of mind” for her in the 2026 election cycle.
Max Himstreet ’28, a member of Dartmouth Democrats, was also at the polls. He told The Dartmouth that he supports Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H.-2 because of her “service and dedication” to veterans and “her stance against the current presidential administration.”
“She really cares about this community,” Himstreet said. “I’ve seen her going around knocking on doors for hours and hours and I respect her work ethic.”
Jesse Fitzelle-Jones ’27, who chairs N.H. College Democrats and serves as the policy director of Dartmouth’s chapter, was volunteering for Manzur’s senate campaign in his personal capacity. Manzur asked him to join her campaign, which he did after seeing an image online of a Palestinian child “in the middle of a pile of rubble” last August, Fitzelle-Jones said.
Fitzelle-Jones said Israel is committing a “genocide” in Gaza and he strongly opposes Pappas’s stance on Israel. In July, Pappas voted “present” on an amendment to end all aid to Israel. Goodlander was one of 104 representatives who voted yes. Fitzelle-Jones said he would vote for Pappas if he advanced to the general election.
Fitzelle-Jones said that while “anything can happen” in today’s primary, he has seen an “incredible” increase in support and attention for Manzur’s campaign in the past few weeks. He argued that Manzur’s progressive platform, including Medicare for all and ending aid to Israel, is popular with independents and unengaged voters.
“They want something new,” he said. “They want something fresh, kind of an outsider to come in and advocate for what they believe in. And she’s been there … She was struggling really for a lot of her life.”
Manzur, who emigrated from Bangladesh when she was in high school, holds a Ph.D. in biochemistry and molecular biology and “thinks like a scientist,” Fitzelle-Jones added.
9:00 a.m.: Rep. Maggie Goodlander visits the polls
Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H.-2, and her staff members visited the polls at Hanover High this morning. In an interview with The Dartmouth, she said she plans to “hit as many” polling locations as possible today.
Goodlander faces a primary challenge from progressive N.H. State Rep. Paige Beauchemin, D-Nashua. Goodlander — a one-term congressperson who previously served in the Navy, clerked for the Supreme Court, worked for the Justice Department and is married to former National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan — said she was “not an establishment politician,” which Beauchemin has called her.
“I know how government works, and I’ve been putting that experience into every day on this job,” Goodlander said. “We’ve been a part of more lawsuits to hold the Trump administration accountable, and to make sure that New Hampshire gets what is owed to the people of the state, from funding for our public schools, to mission critical funding for research at places like Dartmouth, to the healthcare funding that keeps our rural community health centers and hospitals in operation right now, in a moment of genuine crisis.”
7:40 a.m.: Initial voter turnout
Jared Gonzalez Arce / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Turnout at the polls has been sparse so far.
Hanover town moderator Jeremy Eggleton said 38 voters have come through the polls at this point. The voting process has been running “smoothly,” with no “abnormal turnout” expected. Voter turnout “varies” throughout the day, he added.
“We'll get a surge after 3 p.m. when the sports teams at the College finish practice and the coaches tell them all to come over and vote,” Eggleton said.
7:00 a.m.: Polls open at Hanover High gymnasium
Iris WeaverBell / The Dartmouth Senior Staff
Polls for the 2026 New Hampshire primaries are now open in the Hanover High School gymnasium at 41 Lebanon St. Polls will close at 7 p.m.
Voters who are registered as either Democrat or Republican will choose candidates from that party to advance to the general election on Nov. 3. The governor’s seat, one Senate seat, both House seats, Executive Council District 2, state House and state Senate seats and Grafton County officials’ races are on ballots today.
Following Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s, D-N.H., retirement, New Hampshire is key to Democrats’ effort to control the Senate after the 2026 midterms.
Former U.S. Senator John E. Sununu, brother and son of former governors Chris Sununu and John H. Sununu, is favored to defeat former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown and six other candidates for the Republican nomination today.
U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H.-1, and progressive scientist and first-time candidate Karishma Manzur face off in the Democratic primary today. Pappas led Manzur by 13 points in an Aug. 26 University of New Hampshire poll, down from a 46-point gap in April.
A poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire suggested Sununu would narrowly lead Pappas if the two advance to the general election. He would be the state’s first Republican senator since former senator and current governor Kelly Ayotte was elected in 2010.
Ayotte is running for reelection for the first time. Agriculture worker and carpenter Shaun Fife and Goffstown, N.H. resident Bob Wayne McClory are challenging her for the Republican nomination. In the 2024 general election, Ayotte beat out former Manchester, N.H., mayor Joyce Craig with 53% of the vote after receiving an endorsement from her predecessor, Chris Sununu.
Attorney Cinde Warmington, who represented District 2 on New Hampshire’s Executive Council from 2021 to 2025, is the only Democrat on the ballot to face Ayotte in the General Election. Warmington ran for governor in 2024 and lost to Craig in the primary.
The race for New Hampshire’s second Congressional District is projected to be a rematch of 2024 between Lily Tang Williams, a Republican, and current one-term Rep. Maggie Goodlander, who defeated Williams by 6% in 2024. Today, Williams faces stone mason Michael Anthoy Callis, entrepreneur Dan Nicholson and construction business owner Victor Orlando. Progressive State Rep. Paige Beauchemin, D-Nashua, is challenging Goodlander.
All primaries for State Senate and House elections as well as Grafton County officials are uncontested.
Iris WeaverBell ’28 is a reporter and editor. She is from Portland, Ore., and is majoring in economics and minoring in public policy.
Jared Gonzalez Arce '29 is a news reporter from California majoring in history. Out of The D, Jared is in surf club and loves music.

sources.news_title: Pappas and Sununu prevail in New Hampshire primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate • Rhode Island Current
sources.text:
Pappas and Sununu prevail in New Hampshire primaries, setting up expensive fight for U.S. Senate
Chris Pappas (left) and John Sununu (right) will face off in what promises to be a very expensive U.S. Senate race. (Left: Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin; Right: Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November against Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu to be U.S. senator, after the two candidates prevailed in their respective primaries Tuesday.
The results, projected by the Associated Press shortly after 8 p.m., solidified what will likely be a bare-knuckled, expensive general election fight for the Senate seat, which is open after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement.
Polls suggest the contest between Pappas, the current representative for the 1st Congressional District, and Sununu could be close, and both candidates had been positioning themselves for the general election months before the primary. As the polling has tightened, the race has taken on increasing significance to Democrats’ chances to flip control of the U.S. Senate, with Pappas’s shrinking advantage drawing national attention.
In winning his primary, Sununu held off a challenge from Scott Brown, the former U.S. senator from Massachusetts who has since moved to New Hampshire, after Brown attempted to align himself with President Donald Trump and run to Sununu’s right. Trump ultimately endorsed Sununu in February, spurning Brown and propelling Sununu into a lead Brown could never overcome.
Pappas, meanwhile, bested Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist from Exeter and first-time candidate who ran as a progressive. Manzur called for universal health care and attacked Pappas for his prior support of Israel; Pappas has since told the Bulletin he wanted “a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.”
In a statement after his victory, Sununu signaled awareness that the general election fight would be centered on the cost of living.
“We will keep listening, keep working, and stay laser-focused on the economy, jobs, and making life more affordable,” Sununu said in the statement.
“We will clean up Washington and hold politicians in both parties accountable,” Sununu continued. “I’ll push term limits, make Congress pay for the full cost of their healthcare, and cut Congress’ pay if they vote to shut down the government.”
Pappas had a similar message. “Everywhere I go, I hear the same thing: Life is too damn expensive,” he said in a victory speech Tuesday night, citing U.S.-led tariffs affecting businesses, the reduction of healthcare subsidies, and high gas and grocery prices.
“Donald Trump thinks all of this is just a hoax. In fact, he says we’re living in a golden age,” Pappas said. “Well, I think he’s living on another planet because does this feel like a golden age to you?”
Both candidates had decisive victories: Just before 9 p.m., Pappas commanded 62.5% of the vote compared to Manzur’s 35.4%; around the same time, Sununu had taken 69.1% of the vote compared to Brown’s 25.6%, according to the Associated Press.
This story was originally produced by New Hampshire Bulletin, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Rhode Island Current, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

sources.news_title: Former US Sen. Sununu to face US Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire Senate race
sources.text:
CONCORD, N.H. — Republican John E. Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas will compete for an open U.S. Senate seat in New Hampshire in a race that has emerged as one of a handful around the country that could determine control of the chamber in November.
Sununu, a former U.S. senator, and Pappas, a member of the U.S. House, are vying to replace U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, whose decision not to seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races. Both entered their respective party primaries as strong front-runners and now have just eight weeks to make their case to general election voters.
Republicans view the seat as an opportunity to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber, and keeping New Hampshire in their column is a critical part of that effort.
In other top races, Stefany Shaheen, Shaheen's daughter, won a close primary and will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo in the race to fill Pappas' open seat in the 1st Congressional District. The 2nd Congressional District will feature a matchup between U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat seeking her second term, and Republican Lily Tang Williams.
Familiar names will compete in November for open Senate seat
Pappas, who is giving up his seat in the 1st Congressional District after four terms, defeated four other candidates, including democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who had been gaining on him in recent weeks.
Speaking to supporters at his family's restaurant in Manchester, he quickly sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu even though Sununu called him “a loser” during the 2024 presidential campaign.
“While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters,” said Pappas, whose campaign also quickly posted a negative ad on social media calling Sununu “a sequel we can't afford.”
“We've got to turn the page on Donald Trump's reckless leadership, on corruption, on the rigged economy and on costs, and this is not the time to turn it back to a failed politician from the past," he said at his victory party.
Sununu, who spent six years in the U.S. House and one term in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008, called Pappas a career politician who has held office for virtually his entire adult life.
“He’s not an independent voice for New Hampshire,” Sununu said at his victory party at a Manchester ski area. “Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire.”
Sununu defeated seven other Republicans to win the primary, including former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, who accused him of coasting on his name. Sununu's father and younger brother are both former governors.
Jim Loomis, 83, of Bow, said he backed Brown in 2014 but not on Tuesday because “he never got traction back again.” He acknowledged Sununu had been out of politics for even longer but still voted for him.
“I think what he’s done for work over the years has kept him close enough to what’s going on, and then with his family ties, I just think he’s got a more stable base,” Loomis said.
Senator's daughter survives tight contest for 1st District nomination
Stefany Shaheen and Maura Sullivan were the leading candidates among seven seeking the Democratic nomination in the 1st District.
Shaheen is a former city councilor in Portsmouth. She founded a business to help people with chronic medical conditions after one of her daughters was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. She also is part of a bio-tech initiative in New Hampshire to advance regenerative medicine.
Speaking to her supporters Tuesday night before the race was called, Shaheen said she was campaigning to “take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs, the skyrocketing costs families are facing in New Hampshire and across the country.” But she also said running against the president wouldn’t be enough, that she would give voters a reason to turn out for the general election.
“We can bring the real change that’s needed, starting with healthcare, starting with Medicare for all,” she said.
Sullivan is a retired Marine and Iraq War veteran who served as an assistant secretary at the Department of Veterans Affairs under President Barack Obama. A vice chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, Sullivan ran for the 1st District seat in 2018, losing in an 11-candidate primary to Pappas in his first congressional bid.
Her campaign did not immediately return a call and email seeking a response after Shaheen won. Earlier in the night, Sullivan addressed her supporters and thanked them for their hard work during the campaign.
